NERON. Sestercio. (Ae. 26,66g/35mm). 65 d.C. Lugdunum. Anv: NERO CLAVD CAESAR AVG GER P M TR P IMP P P. Busto laureado a derecha de Nerón. Rev: CONG DAT POP. Nerón sentado en estrado, delante oficial ofreciendo congiarum a un ciudadano en las escaleras con un niño detrás, al fondo Minerva sosteniendo lechuza y lanza junto a Libertas sosteniendo Tesera. (RIC 434). MBC+. Retocado. Muy raro ejemplar.Cuenta Suetonio que “nació Nerón en Anzio, nueve meses después de la muerte de Tiberio, el 18 de las calendas de enero al salir el sol”. El último emperador de la dinastía Julio-Claudia y uno de los emperadores romanos con peor “prensa” de toda la historia del Imperio. Persecuciones sobre los cristianos, incendio de Roma en el 64 d.C., asesinatos varios, entre ellos el de su hermano Británico o su madre Agripina, son algunas de las acusaciones que tradicionalmente la historia ha lanzado sobre éste. Buena culpa de esta fama proviene de los escritos de los historiadores coetáneos y/o posteriores como el ya mencionado Suetonio, Tácito o Dion Casio quienes presentaron, al emperador como un auténtico tirano. Cabe reseñar que esta tradicional y simple interpretación ha sido y está siendo puesta en duda en la actualidad, o al menos, existe la corriente que también nos presenta otra vertiente de la figura del emperador, la de un dirigente querido por las clases populares, preocupado por la cultura, las artes o las pruebas deportivas.Desde el punto de vista estrictamente económico o numismático, bajo el gobierno de Nerón se llevó a cabo una importante reforma monetaria en el 64 d.C. que tuvo como objetivo el ampliar la oferta nominal de dinero para evitar la insolvencia del Estado. Básicamente su reforma se centró en reducir el peso teórico tanto del áureo como del denario, así como la pureza de este último y poner en circulación a las denominaciones subsidiarias en oricalco. Esta última medida fue abandonada poco tiempo después ya que este tipo de monedas no fueron nunca aceptadas por el pueblo, pero las dos primeras permanecieron y pervivieron a través de los años. Respecto al estilo de los retratos acuñados en las diferentes piezas, éstos evolucionan, en un claro proceso de realismo artístico, desde el de un joven, ya obeso, y laureado con corona cívica, hasta el de un adulto de duras facciones de los últimos años de reinado.

Rev: Tito estante a derecha sobre carro tirado por cuádriga triunfal. (RIC 498). MBC+/MBC. Retocado. Muy raro ejemplar.A pesar de su corto mandato, fue solo emperador romano dos años, entre el 79 y el 81d.C, y de que bajo éste, ocurrieron varias calamidades que han pasado a la historia como la erupción del Vesubio y el gran incendio que asoló Roma, lo cierto es que es un emperador al que la historiografía siempre trató bien: de gran bondad y generosidad gozó de una enorme popularidad entre otras cosas por la labor de reconstrucción que llevó a cabo en la Roma asolada. Respecto a su numismática, en una primera etapa el retrato sigue la línea de su predecesor, Vespasiano, pero después los rasgos parecen dulcificarse un tanto, aunque dentro de un realismo que no perdona, por ejemplo, la cierta contundencia de su físico.

Rarísimo y probablemente inédita variante de leyenda.Dos caballos y un solo jinete que porta, en lugar de la tradicional palma, una caetra (escudo típico celta) son los elementos más característicos de estas piezas cuya representación ha sido tradicionalmente atribuida a los Dioscuros. Un jinete que siempre cabalga a la izquierda enseñando el escudo mientras que con la mano derecha guía al otro caballo. La gran cantidad de denarios acuñados bajo esta ceca responde a su prolongada acuñación a lo largo y ancho de todo el siglo II a.C con el objetivo de sufragar los pagos de las tropas que combatían las continuas revueltas lusitanas y celtíberas.

POMPEYO, el Grande. Denario. (Ar. 3,78g/19mm). 46-45 a.C. Hispania. (FFC 1; Crawford 469a). Anv: Cabeza de Palas a derecha, alrededor leyenda: M POBLICI LEG PRO PR, todo dentro de gráfila de puntos y rayas. Rev: Pompeyo de pie a izquierda, con un pie sobre proa de barco, entregando una palma a la Bética de pie a derecha con escudo y dos jabalinas, alrededor leyenda: CN MAGNVS IMP. SC-. Vano de acuñación en reverso. Bonito y raro ejemplar.Durante los dos años (47-45 a.C) que estuvo en Hispania, Cneo Pompeyo hijo, hijo mayor de Cneo Pompeyo Magno acuñó dos series de denarios de plata (RRC 469–470) y una de ases de bronce (RRC 471), todo ellos en el marco de la guerra civil que enfrentó a C. Julio César contra el Senado. Estos denarios presentan diferentes variantes en función de los reversos: algunos presentan como grafila puntos y cuentas mientras que otros presentan únicamente puntos. Hay autores que han querido ver también diferencias estilísticas en ellos, diferenciando un estilo bello y un estilo crudo en estas acuñaciones. Pero no acaban aquí las variantes, Villaronga y Benages citan diferenciaciones en las leyendas e incluso, volviendo a la iconografía, hay autores para los que la imagen representada en el anverso es Palas mientras que para otros es Roma. García-Bellido considera que la figura femenina sería, por su postura mayestática la personificación de una divinidad y no de una ciudad o provincia como en otros casos, debido a que no acude ni se arrodilla ante el emperador que recibe el homenaje.

Bonito ejemplar.Definimos a la gens como un conjunto de familias que descendían o creían descender de un antepasado común y que tenían en común divinidades, costumbres y territorio. En el caso de la Scribonia es el brocal, perfil que lo rodea para dotarle de seguridad, del pozo (Puteal Escribonium o Scribonianum) el motivo iconográfico más utilizado en sus acuñaciones y hacen alusión a su construcción en el atrio de Minerva por parte de Escribonio, según relata Festo. Bonus Eventus, en el anverso, es la Diosa de la buena suerte y especialmente invocada en el inicio de un viaje. Existen variantes de esta pieza en función de si en lugar de tenazas en el
descripcion_reverso: aparece un martillo o bien un cincel o buril en lugar de éstos.

descripcion_anverso: ★ Extremely rare, and highy unusual with the owl raising its left wing ★ PHILISTIA. Azotos (Ashdod). Circa 420-350 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 9 mm, 0.68 g, 12 h). Head of Athena to right, with eastern-style coiffure surmounted by a helmet crest.
descripcion_reverso: Owl standing right, head facing, left wing uplifted; to left, 𐡀 (ʾ in Aramaic); to right, 𐡔 (Š in Aramaic) above head of a horse to right; all within guilloche-pattern square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal I.1Ob corr. ( this coin, but eastern-style coiffure not noted). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 2 corr. ( same dies, but eastern-style coiffure not noted). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare, apparently one of just three known examples of this highly interesting issue. Nicely toned and well struck on a full flan. Minor die break on the obverse, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.This piece is remarkable in two respects. First, it appears hitherto to have gone unnoticed that Athena is not wearing a full helmet decorated with three olive leaves and a palmette on the bowl, but that her head is instead rendered as a hybrid combination of eastern-style coiffure and helmet crest. A close parallel is provided by lot 12 (Gitler & Tal II.13D) below.Second, we encounter here a striking variation on the Attic owl: it raises its left wing, lending the design an entirely new sense of dynamism. On the corresponding drachms, moreover, the left wing terminates in a horned (?) lion’s head (Gitler & Tal I.1D), a charming detail that could hardly be accommodated on the smaller mʾhs. descripcion_anverso: ★ Extremely rare and with fascinating iconography ★ PHILISTIA. Azotos (Ashdod). Circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 16 mm, 3.32 g, 12 h). Female head with long hair to left, wearing a crested Corinthian-style helmet, its facial section rendered as the face of a long-bearded man to left.
descripcion_reverso: Bearded male figure (Bes?) advancing right, head facing, with two pairs of wings, the upper pair straight, the lower pair curved; to upper right, 𐡀𐡔 (ʾŠ in Aramaic); to upper left, 𐡃𐡃 (DD in Aramaic); in lower left field, head of a horse to left; in lower right field, head of an uncertain animal to right; all within dotted square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal II.3Dc corr. ( this coin, but described as a male head to left). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 10 var. ( same dies, but with 𐡁 (B in Aramaic) added later to the female's cheek). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare and among the finest known examples of this fascinating issue. Beautifully toned and with highly complex and unusual iconography. Slightly rough and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.The iconography of this piece is exceptional. The Philistian die engravers’ fondness for hidden images and optical illusions is strikingly evident on the obverse: the ‘facial section’ of the Corinthian helmet is rendered as the head of an older man with a carefully shaped long beard. Gitler & Tal describe the principal head, facing left, as male; perhaps they saw in the image a deliberate play on stages of life, in which the face of an inexperienced youth is concealed beneath the martial countenance of a mature, bearded man. More likely, however, the principal head should be understood as female, analogous to the depictions of Athena on Corinthian Pegasoi, which clearly served as the model for the type; the intended effect would then be a play on gender rather than on age. Unlike the Greek prototypes of the fifth century BC, where the hair is usually straight and gathered into a knot, the hair on the Philistian imitation is rendered as a wavy eastern-style coiffure.The reverse is no less striking. The bearded male figure with two pairs of wings cannot be identified with certainty. While the frontal, mask-like head recalls Bes, the two pairs of wings place the figure within a broader Near Eastern repertoire of winged protective beings. Four-winged forms of Bes are attested in Phoenicianizing contexts, and the motif also invites comparison with Mesopotamian figures such as Pazuzu, whose developed iconography includes two pairs of wings, as well as with the winged genii or apkallu of Neo-Assyrian art and the four-winged protective figure of Achaemenid Pasargadae. The figure on the present coin is therefore perhaps best understood not as a straightforward image of Bes, but as a local Philistian hybrid, combining an Egyptianizing, Bes-like head with the wider Near Eastern iconography of winged protective beings. descripcion_anverso: ★ An extremely rare Rbʾ Šql from Ashdod ★ PHILISTIA. Azotos (Ashdod). Circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 14 mm, 3.69 g, 9 h). Janiform head composed of a bearded male head to left and a female head to right; above, recumbent bovine left, head turned back to right; all within circular guilloche-pattern border.
descripcion_reverso: Recumbent bovine right, head turned back to left, an owl concealed within its body; below, two confronted ram heads; above, 𐡔𐡃𐡃 (ŠDD in Aramaic); all within dotted square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal II.5Dc ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 12-13 ( same dies ). Mildenberg, Palästina, pl. LV, 20 ( same dies ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare, very well centered, and nicely toned. Minor roughness and with the usual reverse test cut, otherwise, good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.An interesting minor detail of this beautiful coin is the small owl concealed in the forepart of the bovine’s body on the reverse – a charming echo of the profound influence exerted by the Athenian owls on the coinage of the Levant and beyond. Another playful element is found in the ethnic legend: while only ŠDD is written, the bovine’s head, turned back to the left, may be understood as a pictographic substitute for the missing initial aleph, thus completing the city name as ʾŠDD, Ashdod. Here, the die-cutter appears to allude to the origin of the letter-name aleph / ʾalp, meaning 'ox' in West Semitic, and to the letter’s pictographic ancestry, generally thought to go back ultimately to an ox-head sign in the early alphabetic tradition. descripcion_anverso: ★ A highly interesting rendering of the bull's horns as a crescent ★ PHILISTIA. Azotos (Ashdod). Circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 15 mm, 3.81 g, 6 h). Janiform head composed of a bearded male head to left and a female head to right.
descripcion_reverso: Forepart of a recumbent bovine right, its horns forming a crescent, an owl concealed within its body; before, 𐡃 (D in Aramaic); all within dotted square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal II.7Da ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 17 ( same obverse die ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare and undoubtedly the finest of a very few known examples. Beautifully toned and with a wonderful reverse. The obverse struck slightly off center and with a minor test cut on the reverse, otherwise, good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.As in lots 4 and 5 above, the bull’s head is here likewise to be read as a pictographic aleph, yielding the ethnic ʾ[Š]D. Particularly noteworthy – and, to our knowledge, hitherto unnoticed in the scholarship – is the rendering of the bull’s horns as a crescent. Whether intended as a purely formal device or as a sacral allusion, the motif resonates with a well-established ancient Near Eastern association between the bull, the crescent, and the lunar sphere, especially in connection with the moon god Sîn/Nanna. The type may therefore play simultaneously on letter, image, and cultic symbol: the ox-head as aleph, the ox as emblem, and its horns as a lunar crescent. descripcion_reverso: Facing female head, with 'Egyptianizing' hair or wig; in fields below, 𐡀-𐡔 ('Š in Aramaic); all within dotted square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal II.8Da = Mildenberg, Palästina, pl. LV, 23 ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 19 ( same dies ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare and very likely the finest known example. A beautiful piece with an exceptional rendering of the striking 'woman at the window' motif. Traces of overstriking and with a test cut and a flan fault on the reverse, otherwise, about extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.The striking female head, with its intense gaze, on the reverse of this magnificent coin may be understood against the background of the well-known 'woman at the window' motif, frequently encountered in Levantine-Phoenician ivory carving of the early 1st millennium BCE (on the motif, see I. J. Winter, The ‘Woman at the Window': Iconography and Inferences of a Motif in First-Millennium B.C. Levantine Ivory Carving, in: J. Aruz and M. Seymour (eds.), Assyria to Iberia: Art and Culture in the Iron Age, New York 2016, pp. 180–193).The motif is characterized by the frontal presentation of a female head or bust within an architectural frame, often with a heavy Egyptianizing coiffure and a gaze directed straight at the viewer. Its interpretation is not entirely clear: some scholars have seen in it the representation of a goddess, perhaps Astarte, while others have interpreted it as a richly adorned elite woman, a queen, or a female figure with cultic associations.On the present coin, the Philistine artist has adapted this visual idea to the numismatic medium with remarkable assurance: the 'window' from which the female head, wearing a heavy Egyptianizing wig, confronts the viewer is formed by the dotted square within the quadratum incusum. descripcion_anverso: ★ The finest of just two known, and with exceptional iconography ★ PHILISTIA. Azotos (Ashdod). Circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 16 mm, 3.83 g, 12 h). Bearded male head to right, hair gathered at the back and with a horn- or animal-ear-like projection on the forehead.
descripcion_reverso: Bovine walking right, head lowered and raising right foreleg, an owl concealed within its body; to upper right, miniature male (?) head to right; above bovine, 𐡀𐡔 (ʾŠ in Aramaic); all within square guilloche-pattern border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal II.9Da = YC p. 144, Fig. V.13 ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 21 = Mildenberg, Palästina, pl. LV, 22 = Shoshana I 20045 ( same dies ). Sofaer -. Of the highest rarity, and the finest of apparently just two known examples. An exceptionally charming and very well-preserved coin, beautifully toned, perfectly centered, and with remarkable detail. Very light roughness, otherwise, extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.The remarkable archaic head on the obverse is usually described – sometimes with a question mark – as a satyr head, presumably on account of its large, staring eye, snub nose, and, above all, the curious horn- or ear-like projection on the forehead, which has apparently been interpreted as a pointed animal ear of the kind familiar from Greek depictions of satyrs. This interpretation, however, is not without difficulties: in Greek art, a satyr’s ear, no matter how prominently rendered, would be expected in its anatomically correct position, not at the hairline above the forehead. Its placement rather suggests a horn; yet this, too, is not entirely convincing, since horns are normally set higher on the head or at the temples. Even in the case of Zeus Ammon, the characteristic ram’s horn is placed laterally, behind or above the ear, not on the forehead. The image therefore remains enigmatic. It is perhaps best understood as one of those hybrid visual creations in which Philistine artists freely combined Greek, Persian, Egyptianizing, and local elements.The reverse, too, reflects this taste for visual hybridity: once again, an Attic owl is concealed within the body of the bull, while the small male (?) head in the upper right field adds an additional human element to the predominantly animal composition; compare also lot 16 below. descripcion_anverso: ★ Only the second known specimen of this previously unrecognized variety, and with a beautiful facing owl ★ PHILISTIA. Askalon (Ashkelon). Circa 420-350 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 10 mm, 0.71 g, 6 h). Female head to right, the hair drawn back and tied into a ponytail, wearing a pearl necklace; before, V-shaped symbols within circular guilloche-pattern border.
descripcion_reverso: Owl standing facing, wings spread; to upper left, 𐤍𐤀 ('N in Phoenician); above the owl's head and below its feet, hieroglyphic sign for a ripple of water (?); lotus buds on four sides; all within incuse square. Fischer-Bossert, Philistian, 6e ( this coin ). Gitler & Tal III.4Ob corr. ( same dies, but necklace and obverse ornaments not noted, and the hieroglyphic sign for water below not above the owl). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -, cf. 35 ( same reverse die ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare, one of just six known examples, and only the second known specimen of this previously unrecognized variety. A magnificent piece, beautifully toned and with exceptional detail. Uncleaned horn silver and with a small die break on the obverse, otherwise, extremely fine.Ex Leu 75, 25 October 1999, 1305 (with original ticket).This piece is remarkable not only for its exceptional preservation, but also for its considerable numismatic importance, since it represents a previously unrecognized variety. On the obverse, V-shaped symbols with terminal dots are visible between the nose, mouth, and chin of the female head and the dotted border. On the die-identical example Gitler & Tal III.4Ob (see lot 15 below), struck from a worn obverse die, these symbols are barely discernible, especially as they partly fell outside the flan. This explains why III.4Oa and III.4Ob have hitherto been described as a single type.The symbols recall what Gitler & Tal describe as the 'hieroglyphic sign for a ripple of water' appearing on the reverse above the owl; on the obverse, by contrast, the individual elements are separated by distinct spaces, whereas on the reverse they form a continuous motif. In fact, this sign appears below the owl’s feet rather than above them. Its close resemblance to the newly identified obverse symbols raises the question whether it should be understood as a decorative motif rather than as a hieroglyphic sign. Finally, our piece is also significant in that the likewise previously overlooked pearl necklace is clearly visible here. The obverse, by contrast, with its magnificent janiform head, was probably inspired by the late Archaic coinage of Tenedos; cf. Nomos 1 (2009), 95 = Triton XV (2012), 1002 = Numismatica Ars Classica 154 (2025), 1246. descripcion_anverso: ★ Imitating Akanthos, and arguably the finest of just five known examples ★ PHILISTIA. Gaza. Circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 15 mm, 3.78 g, 6 h). Lion to right, attacking a bull collapsing to left; below, uncertain symbol (shrimp to right?); all within guilloche-pattern circular border.
descripcion_reverso: Forepart of a horse right, forelock tied up with a ribbon into an upright tuft; in upper left field, 𐡏𐡆 (ʿZ in Aramaic); all within dotted square border within incuse square. BMC Palestine pl. XIX, 15 ( same dies ). Gitler & Tal VI.9Db ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 132 ( same obverse die ). Shoshana - Sofaer -. Extremely rare, arguably the finest of just five known examples of this wonderful issue. Beautifully toned and with highly interesting iconography. Struck from the usual worn obverse die, otherwise, extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.Finds such as the famous Asyut Hoard show that large quantities of northern Greek and Thraco-Macedonian silver reached the eastern Mediterranean. This movement of silver should probably be seen, at least in part, in connection with Achaemenid control over Thrace and northern Greece from the reign of Dareios I onward; tribute payments, military requirements, and trade relations are also likely to have played an important role. The gravitational pull of the vast Achaemenid Empire was undoubtedly considerable in this respect.For the present coin, this is significant because the obverse, showing a lion bringing down a bull, clearly draws on Akanthian prototypes, examples of which were also prominently represented in the Asyut Hoard (153-193). This supports a dating to the late 5th century BCE and at the same time points to the close connections of the Philistian coastal cities with the Aegean world.It is more difficult to determine the source of inspiration for the horse protome on the reverse. In Greek coinage, the horse-protome motif is widespread, occurring from Thessaly through Thrace to Asia Minor. At the same time, the rendering of the forelock tied up into a topknot finds particularly close parallels in Achaemenid art, for example on the reliefs of the Apadana at Persepolis and on Achaemenid horse-protome rhyta (see Gitler, Achaemenid, pl. III, 16). The coin thus combines elements from different pictorial traditions in a manner characteristic of early Philistian silver coinage. descripcion_anverso: ★ Extremely rare and with a very important overstrike ★ PHILISTIA. Gaza. Circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 17 mm, 3.96 g, 9 h). Youthful female head to right, hair gathered at the back.
descripcion_reverso: Facing head of Bes; in fields, 𐡏-𐡆 (ʿZ in Aramaic); all within dotted square border within incuse square. Fischer-Bossert, Philistian, 32b = Gitler & Tal VI.14Db ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 141 ( same dies ). Mildenberg, Vestigia, pl. XXVII, 25. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare and of great numismatic interest. A beautiful, lightly toned coin and an important overstrike. Traces of overstriking and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, about extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.What makes this piece significant, quite apart from its great rarity, is the evidence of overstriking – evidence that has not previously been discussed in the literature, perhaps because the undertype had not yet been identified. Traces of the earlier coin are visible on both sides. On the reverse, in the beard of Bes, a bearded head right can be made out when the coin is rotated through 240°. On the obverse, the evidence is less immediately legible: a dotted square border within an incuse square is clearly visible, but the main device is almost entirely obscured. The Aramaic letter 𐡏 (ʿAyin), however, can be seen distinctly on the neck of the female head.Taken together, these traces point to an undertype with a bearded male head right on its obverse and, on its reverse, a dotted square border within an incuse square accompanied by the letter 𐡏. This points either to Gitler & Tal V.8D (cf. lot 25 above) or to Gitler & Tal VI.1D (cf. lot 31 above). A close comparison with Gitler & Tal V.8Da specifically confirms the former identification: the laurel-wreathed bearded head, modelled on an Aradian prototype and thus perhaps representing Ba'al-Arwad, corresponds precisely to the visible facial outline on the reverse of the present piece. At the same time, the fine lines of the falcon’s tail feathers can now also be recognized on the obverse, extending from the hair of the female head into the corner of the undertype’s incuse square. The present coin was therefore overstruck on an earlier issue of Gaza, apparently struck from the same dies as the example published as Gitler & Tal V.8Da, and thus provides valuable evidence for the relative chronology of the city’s coinage. descripcion_anverso: ★ Very rare as a type, and of outstanding importance as this unique overstrike ★ PHILISTIA. Gaza. Circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 16 mm, 3.68 g, 2 h). Janiform bearded male head, wearing pearl necklace.
descripcion_reverso: Two opposed griffin-like creatures with elongated, wing-like necks ending in bovine heads; facing female head between them; above, 𐡏𐡆 (ʿZ in Aramaic); all within guilloche-patterned square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal VI.16Db corr. ( this coin, but misdescribed as double struck). Gitler, Johananoff and Tal, Overstrikes, Fig. 6, VI.16Db ( this coin ). Hendin 6009. Jeselsohn 144. Mildenberg, Vestigia, pl. XXV, 34 (with ethnic). Shoshana -. Sofaer 17. Very rare as a type, and of outstanding importance as this unique overstrike. Darkly toned. Somewhat rough and with traces of overstriking, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.When first published, our piece was described as ‘double struck’, and the obverse was illustrated upside down, causing the janiform bearded male head to appear vertically oriented. Closer inspection, however, shows that the coin was not double struck, but clearly overstruck. On the obverse, above the janiform male head, the face of a woman looking upwards is visible; on the reverse, a bearded head can be made out on the right. These traces belong to the obverse and reverse of an earlier coin, namely Gitler & Tal XVI.11D.This anepigraphic type shows a male head on the obverse and a female head on the reverse. Although the overstrike makes die comparison difficult, the undertype nevertheless appears to have been struck from the same dies as Gitler & Tal XVI.11Da. This important discovery now allows this earlier anonymous Philistian coinage to be linked with the later coinage of Gaza, thereby providing an important relative chronology. The coin will shortly be republished and discussed in a forthcoming study of overstrikes by H. Gitler, M. Johananoff, and O. Tal. descripcion_anverso: ★ The symbol of Marnas, chief god and civic deity of Gaza ★ PHILISTIA. Gaza. Circa early 340s-332 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 14 mm, 3.91 g, 1 h). Head of Athena to right, wearing crested Attic helmet decorated with three olive leaves and palmette; on cheek, 𐡌 (M in Aramaic).
descripcion_reverso: Owl standing right, head facing; to left, olive sprig and crescent; to right, Α ☉Ε. Fischer-Bossert, Philistian, 16c = Gitler & Tal V.25Dc ( this coin ). Hendin 6010. Jeselsohn 101 ( same dies ). Mildenberg, Vestigia, pl. XXIV, 7 ( same dies ). Shoshana II 20006-20007 ( same dies ). Sofaer -. Beautifully toned and with an unusually attractive obverse. The reverse weakly struck, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.The letter mem (𐡌) on Athena's cheek is the symbol of Marnas, the chief god and civic deity of Gaza, thereby securing the attribution of the drachm to the Philistian coastal city. In the Graeco-Roman period, Marnas was identified with Zeus and worshipped in the city’s famous Marneion. The symbol itself enjoyed a remarkable iconographic continuity: already attested on the present issue, dating to the early 340s-332 BCE, it remained the emblem of the god and the city for at least six centuries, still appearing on the last Roman provincial coins of Gaza, struck in 241/2 CE under Gordian III (238-244). See also lot 426 below, a coin of Hadrian showing the Temple of Marnas.Unlike other Philistian coinages of the Athenian type, which are generally thought to have continued into the early years of Macedonian rule, the coinage of Gaza provides a clear terminus ante quem. In 332 BCE, Alexander the Great besieged the strongly fortified city during his advance towards Egypt. After a siege of several weeks, involving extensive earthworks and the use of siege engines, Gaza was captured by the Macedonians; the ancient sources report heavy losses among the defenders and the enslavement of part of the population. Gaza’s autonomous coinage therefore most likely ceased with, or at the latest by, the Macedonian conquest of the city in 332 BCE. descripcion_anverso: ★ Extremely rare, and inspired by the Egyptian ba-bird? ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Athenian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 10 mm, 0.59 g, 3 h). Head of Athena to right, wearing crested Attic helmet decorated with three olive leaves and palmette.
descripcion_reverso: Human-headed bird standing right; to left, olive sprig; to right, [A]●E; all within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XIII.1Oa ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare, the finest of apparently just three known examples. Darkly toned and struck on a broad flan. Die break on the reverse, otherwise, good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.Gitler and Tal have raised the question of whether the human-headed bird – a variation on the Athenian owl – on the reverse of this unusual issue was inspired by the Egyptian ba-bird. In Egyptian thought, the ba was not a 'soul' in the modern sense, but rather one of the non-physical aspects of a person, associated above all with mobility: after death, it could leave the tomb and later return to the mummy. For this reason, it was often depicted as a bird with a human head, sometimes with human arms as well. Human-headed birds, however, are also attested in other cultural spheres, such as the sirens of Greek mythology or siren- and harpy-like figures from Asia Minor, especially Lycia. As so often in Philistine coinage, with its syncretistic imagery and playful visual language, the interpretation ultimately remains open. descripcion_anverso: ★ A wonderful apotropaic Rbʾ Šql ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Athenian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 14 mm, 3.86 g, 12 h). Head of Athena to right, wearing crested Attic helmet decorated with three olive leaves and palmette.
descripcion_reverso: Hybrid head composed of a bearded male head to right, with a facing gorgoneion (?), tongue protruding, emerging from the back of the male head at a right angle; all within dotted square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XIII.5Dd ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 216 ( same dies ). Mildenberg, Palästina, pl. 58, 63 ( same obverse die ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare, one of apparently just five known examples. Boldly struck from fresh dies. Athena's nose off flan and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, about extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.Mildenberg interpreted the facing head on the reverse of this drachm as a representation of the Egyptian god Bes, whose image occupies a prominent place in Philistine coinage (Mildenberg, Palästina, p. 384). The authors of the first volume of the Jeselsohn Collection, however, argue that the image should instead be understood as a gorgoneion: the open mouth, bared teeth, and protruding tongue are clearly visible, all characteristic features of an archaic gorgoneion.This identification does not necessarily imply that the full Greek myth of Perseus and Medusa was intended here. The gorgoneion was not confined to Greek art, but belonged to a broader eastern Mediterranean visual tradition and may have reached Philistine coinage through Phoenician or other Levantine channels. It should therefore not be understood simply as a Greek mythological borrowing. The hybrid image probably carried an apotropaic meaning: the fearsome gorgoneion may have served as a protective device, while its visual assimilation to Bes, the ancient Egyptian protective god, may have been deliberate (cf. the note on lot 101 below). descripcion_reverso: Winged and horned lion-griffin seated to right within cable-pattern border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XIII.15Da ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 223 ( same reverse die ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Of the highest rarity, one of just two known examples. Beautifully toned and with a highly interesting reverse. The obverse struck slightly off center and with considerable edge filing, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.When Gitler and Tal published their important corpus of Philistine coinage in 2006, only the present specimen of this remarkable type was known to them. With the publication of the first volume of the highly significant Jeselsohn Collection in 2024, a second example has now come to light, struck from the same reverse die. The animal is described there as a 'lion or lynx', but may perhaps be more precisely understood as a lion-griffin, a type of composite creature especially familiar from Achaemenid imperial art (see also lots 115-116 below). Comparable representations are found, for example, on the famous griffin friezes from the palace of Darius I at Susa, now in the Louvre, as well as on gold objects from the Oxus Treasure, such as BM 123929. Breaks in plating on the obverse and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.All known specimens of this type are silver-plated. These are by no means unofficial contemporary forgeries; rather, the coins were deliberately produced as such. Gitler and Tal record an example on which the entire silver plating has been lost (XXIII.16Db), leaving only the blurred outlines of the design visible on the bronze core. In fact, the present specimen is the best preserved example known. Although the plating on the obverse has also been largely lost, the reverse is almost completely preserved, despite the test cut. descripcion_anverso: ★ The head of Themistokles? ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Athenian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 11 mm, 0.66 g, 12 h). Bearded male head (Themistokles?) to right, in the style of Athena, wearing crested Attic helmet decorated with three olive leaves and palmette.
descripcion_reverso: Two opposed seated lions, owls concealed within their bodies; below, two opposed dolphins; all within dotted square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XIII.22Oa ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 230-231 ( same dies ). Mildenberg, Vestigia, pl. XXVI, 8 ( same dies ). Shoshana - Sofaer -. Very rare and of great interest, with a beautiful reverse. Struck from a somewhat worn obverse die, otherwise, good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.Gitler and Tal describe this obverse as a 'bearded helmeted head of Athena'. Bearded heads are, of course, widespread in Philistian coinage, but they normally do not wear helmets. One might therefore be tempted to see it as one of the iconographic hybrid forms so characteristic of Philistian coinage. Greek coinage, however, offers a potentially closer parallel: the coinage struck at Magnesia on the Maeander by the famous Athenian naval commander Themistokles. As von Mosch has recently argued, the depictions of a bearded man wearing an Attic helmet on these coins are best understood as portraits (Mosch 2022). Their resemblance to the bearded male head on our coin is sufficiently close that, although direct influence cannot be demonstrated, the possibility should at least be considered (Mosch 2022, p. 27).More recently, Mosch has also shown that the coinage of the Lykomidai was far more complex and extensive than previously assumed (Mosch 2025). The close connections between Achaemenid western Asia Minor and the Levant are further illustrated by the coinage of Tissaphernes, satrap of Lydia and Ionia, at Dora (Leu 19 (2025), 96). It is therefore possible that the coinage of Themistokles, an Achaemenid client dynast, was known in Philistia and may have influenced the depiction on our coin. descripcion_anverso: ★ Unique and of great importance, and remarkable for its imposing janiform head ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint (?). Athenian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 14 mm, 3.52 g, 5 h). Janiform bearded male head.
descripcion_reverso: Owl standing right, head facing; to left, olive sprig; to right, Α ☉; all within circular incuse. Gitler & Tal XIV.18Da ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Unique and of great importance. A beautifully toned and impressive coin, remarkable for its imposing janiform head in a distinctively local style. Good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.Janiform heads are frequently depicted on Philistian coins. In most cases, they combine a bearded male face with a female face, a pairing also familiar from Greek coinage, especially that of Tenedos. Types with two bearded male faces are also attested, however, as for example on lot 80 above. Unlike that piece, which stands out for its exceptional, Greek-influenced style, the present specimen is a much more conspicuously local product. Here, the two faces are hardly connected at all, forming a double head rather than a single one. The local artist has rendered the faces in a markedly more rudimentary style, which, with its bulging foreheads, prominent noses and large eyes, appears almost brutalist. As a drachm, this impressive piece is apparently without parallel, since the type is otherwise known exclusively as an obol (see lots 61-62 below). descripcion_anverso: ★ Extremely rare and in spectacular condition, a true gem with remarkable iconography ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Athenian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Half Mʿh = Hemiobol (Silver, 9 mm, 0.34 g, 6 h). Horned head of a griffin to left.
descripcion_reverso: Owl standing right, head facing; to left, olive sprig; to right, AOE; all within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XIV.23HOa corr. ( same dies, obverse described as a 'monster'). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Kraay, Abu Shusheh, 16 and pl. 29, E = Lambert, Palestine, 16 and pl. I, 16 corr. ( same dies, obverse described as an 'elephant's head r. (? or helmet)'). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare and in spectacular condition. A true gem, beautifully toned and sharply struck on excellent silver, with exceptional detail and remarkable iconography. Very minor weakness on the griffin's horn, otherwise, good extremely fine.Ex Leu 75, 25 October 1999, 1315 (with original ticket), and previously from the so-called 'Abu Shusheh hoard' of 1930 (IGCH 1507).This magnificent hemiobol, or half-ma'ah, surely ranks among the most impressive and beautiful Philistian coins known. On tiny dies, the artist has compressed a wealth of detail that stands comparison with the work of the finest Greek die-engravers. The reverse in particular, with its beautifully struck complete incuse square and exceptionally fine owl, immediately evokes the classical Athenian tetradrachms, which exerted such a profound influence on the numismatic iconography of the Levant.The obverse, by contrast, shows a left-facing animal head with horns and beak, which Lambert completely misunderstood and misidentified as an 'elephant’s head r. (? or helmet)'. Kraay had already pointed out this error and at the same time offered a new interpretation, identifying the head as that of a griffin. Gitler and Tal were more cautious, describing it as a 'horned monster’s head'. In this case, however, Kraay’s interpretation should be preferred: comparison with the magnificent gilded Achaemenid rhyton in the British Museum (BM 124081) reveals a striking resemblance. The beak, wide-open eyes, horns, pointed ears, and the suggested plumage above and behind the eye all closely recall the depiction on our coin. Kraay’s identification of the head as that of a griffin therefore seems highly plausible. descripcion_anverso: ★ The most impressive Philistian Rbʾ Šql = Drachm known ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Athenian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 14 mm, 3.38 g, 3 h). Complex hybrid janiform head, with male (?) head facing and female head to right, surmounted by a long-tailed crouching lion to right with reverted head and open jaws; both human heads wearing pearl necklaces; all within circular guilloche-pattern border.
descripcion_reverso: Head of Athena to right, wearing crested Attic helmet decorated with three olive leaves and palmette; in three of the corners, uncertain symbols; all within square guilloche-pattern border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XIV.35Da = Mildenberg, Imagery, pl. III, 52 = Mildenberg, Palästina, pl. LIX, 90 ( this coin ). Hendin 6016 ( same dies ). Jeselsohn 266 = Mildenberg, Vestigia, pl. XXVI, 6 = Shoshana I 20008 ( same dies ). Leu Web Auction 30 (2024), 1097 ( same dies ). Sofaer -. Extremely rare, and by far the finest of just six known examples. A spectacular and iconic coin, certainly the most impressive Philistian drachm known. Attractively toned, perfectly centered and boldly struck on excellent metal; a masterpiece of Levantine art. Test cut on the reverse, otherwise, extremely fine.Ex Leu 72, 12 May 1998, 365 (with original ticket, and illustrated on the front cover!).On this magnificent drachm, or rbʿ šql, the Attic head of Athena appears on the reverse, while the obverse bears an impressive hybrid janiform head. Its intricate and complex iconography is difficult to unravel. Two human faces are clearly visible: a profile face looking right and a frontal face turned toward the viewer. Above them is a long-tailed lion crouching right, with head reverted and jaws open, serving as a headdress. Gitler and Tal also identify a third face looking right between the two heads.Numerous parallels for a janiform head composed of a profile face and a frontal face can be found in Philistian coinage, for example lots 53-54 above; the frontal face also recalls the male three-quarter portraits on lots 58-59. Janiform heads need not be read only in the narrow temporal sense later associated with the Roman Janus. More broadly, the form lends itself to ideas of duality, liminality, heightened vigilance, and the fusion of opposing or complementary elements.In Philistian coinage, where Greek, local and Near Eastern visual traditions are often combined with remarkable freedom, such heads could serve as particularly powerful images of hybrid identity. This applies not only to male-female combinations, but also to types with two male faces, in which the same sense of doubling, ambiguity and intensified presence is preserved. In the present piece, the direct gaze of the frontal face heightens this effect and gives the image a distinctly apotropaic quality: the frontal face does not merely look at the viewer; it confronts the viewer directly. 'I see you' – this unspoken message of the image combines vigilance, protection, strength and the power to ward off harm.Gitler and Tal interpret the head as a combination of a female face to right and a male frontal face. However, the gender attribution of unbearded Philistian faces is notoriously difficult, and the frontal face might also be understood as a frontal rendering of an Athena-like female figure. The two authors further identify, between the two faces, the mouth and nose of another face, which – together with the left eye of the frontal face – would form a third profile looking right (Gitler & Tal pp. 298-299). On closer inspection, however, the supposed nose seems to point left rather than right, so it remains uncertain whether the die-engraver actually intended a third face.The hybrid head is surmounted by a long-tailed lion crouching right, with head reverted and jaws open. Animal headdresses are well attested in ancient art, for example in the lion-skin headdress of Herakles or the elephant-scalp headdresses of various Hellenistic kings. In those cases, however, the animal is present as a trophy or skin; on our coin, by contrast, a living, aggressively animated lion appears, probably further emphasizing the martial and protective power of the hybrid being. Iconographically closer are the frontal Bes heads, each adorned with a lion protome (Gitler & Tal XVIII.8Dc = lot 102 below). Interestingly, these pieces likewise show on the reverse a hybrid head composed of a female face in profile to right and a frontal bearded male face. The close association between Bes and the lion is also indicated by the drachm Gitler & Tal XVIII.5D, whose obverse shows a hybrid head composed of a bearded male head to right and a frontal female or youthful male head, while the reverse shows Bes standing frontally beside an attacking lion. A parallel may also be drawn with Gitler & Tal XVI.21Da (= lot 86 below), which shows a janiform hybrid head composed of a youthful male (?) head to right and a roaring lion’s head to left. A further, more distant comparison is the Oxus aigrette from the Oxus Treasure, an Achaemenid gold ornament in the form of a recumbent lion-griffin with wings, horns and long pointed ears (BM 123924), probably worn in the hair or on a cap.Finally, the Philistian artist seems to have deliberately played with the Athenian model. While the reverse shows a classical Athena with Attic helmet and crest, whose profile appears closely related to the right-facing face on the obverse, the obverse presents a powerful, imaginative and thoroughly local hybrid creature in which Greek, Achaemenid and Levantine elements are fused. The coin thus shows, in the truest sense, two sides of the same coin: on one side the high classical Athena, one of the most famous profile images of the ancient world; on the other, a characteristically Philistian creation of great iconographic complexity and apotropaic force. (with additional symbol in lower right corner). Mildenberg, Palästina, pl. LIX, 90 var. (with additional symbol in lower right corner). Jeselsohn 266 var. = Mildenberg, Vestigia, pl. XXVI, 6 var. = Shoshana I 20008 var. (with additional symbol in lower right corner). Leu Web Auction 30 (2024), 1097 var. (with additional symbol in lower right corner). Sofaer -. The obverse struck slightly off center and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.This piece is the only one in the series struck from a different pair of dies. The dies differ not only stylistically – being executed in a much coarser and more distinctly local manner – but also in one small detail: the absence of the symbol in the lower right corner. The engraver clearly copied the original, stylistically much finer die pair. In doing so, he overlooked the symbol at lower right, perhaps because he was working not from the original dies, but from a coin on which the symbol lay off the flan, as on Jeselsohn 266 = Shoshana 20008. Alternatively, its omission may have been due to wear on the model die, as on lot 68 above, where the symbols are only faintly visible. Whether he copied the symbol in the upper left corner or omitted it as well remains unclear, since the relevant part of the design is off the flan on our coin. descripcion_anverso: ★ Apparently unpublished and surely among the most impressive surviving Philistian coins ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Philistian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 16 mm, 3.69 g, 9 h). Janiform bearded male head, wearing pearl necklace.
descripcion_reverso: Two antithetic griffin-like creatures with elongated, wing-like necks ending in bovine heads; facing female head between them; all within guilloche-patterned square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal -, cf. VI.16D (Gaza). Hendin -, cf. 6009 (Gaza). Jeselsohn -, cf. 144 (Gaza). Leu 19 (2025), 93 ( same dies ). Mildenberg, Vestigia, -, cf. pl. XXV, 34 (Gaza). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Apparently unpublished without the ethnic, apart from the die-matching example in Leu 19 (2025), 93, and by far the finer of the two. A magnificent piece of vigorous style, struck on excellent metal; surely among the most impressive surviving Philistian coins. Very light doubling on the obverse and with a test cut and a small scuff on the reverse, otherwise, nearly extremely fine.Ex Leu 75, 25 October 1999, 1314 (with original ticket).This remarkable coin is closely connected to lot 44 above from Gaza, but lacks the ethnic legend on the reverse. The janiform head on the obverse is also rendered differently, without the continuous horizontal line of hair connecting the two faces that is so characteristic of Gitler & Tal VI.16D. Close parallels for the reverse occur among other anepigraphic types, including Gitler & Tal XXVII.5D, XXVIII.14O and Mildenberg, Vestigia, pl. XXVII, 18. The connection to Gaza is clearly very strong. The absence of the ethnic, however, suggests that the coin may have been issued in a different context, whether under another authority or for another purpose.The piece must rank among the most impressive surviving Philistian coins. The janiform head, with its unusual pairing of two male faces rather than the more familiar male-and-female combination, belongs among the finest achievements of Philistian die engraving. No less remarkable is the reverse, with its two lion-griffins whose necks, transformed into wings ending in bovine heads, enfold the central facing face. As the comparison with lot 115 below shows, the engraver employs another sophisticated visual device: the frontal female head takes the place of the lion-griffins' expected profile heads. The result is a particularly successful example of the interplay between frontal and profile views so characteristic of Philistian coinage. What might otherwise be read as a pair of confronting felines in profile – compare lot 57 above, where the device appears with two lions – is here transformed into two complex hybrid beings framing the central focus of the composition: the frontal, apotropaic female head. Eshel pl. 6, 1 ( same dies ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Mildenberg, Imagery, pl. 2, 29. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare and the finest known example. A beautiful coin with expressive, finely rendered heads and a perfectly centered reverse. Somewhat rough and the obverse struck slightly off center, otherwise, about extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.What is most striking about this coin is the close similarity between the two heads. The only differences are that the obverse head is fully bearded and shown within a circular guilloche border, whereas the reverse head is unbearded and appears within a dotted square border. The facial features, hairstyle and necklace are otherwise identical. We may therefore assume with considerable confidence that the head on the reverse is male as well.The artist may perhaps be playing here with the contrast between youth and age: the bearded, older head on the obverse is answered on the reverse by its youthful counterpart. The deeply impressed incuse square, framed by the dotted border, further enhances this sense of separation, almost as if the reverse offered a second, more distant image of the same figure at an earlier stage of life – a window into the past. descripcion_anverso: ★ Imitating Kyrene, and the only example in private hands ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Philistian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 15 mm, 3.79 g, 9 h). Female head to right, the hair drawn back and tied into a ponytail.
descripcion_reverso: Bearded head of Zeus Ammon to right, with ram's horn over his ear, hair gathered at the back, and wearing pearl necklace, within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XVI.10Da ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare, the finest of just two known examples, and the only one in private hands. Beautifully toned. Die break on the obverse and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.The horn worn by the bearded god on the reverse of this extremely rare issue alludes to Zeus Ammon, the oracular god of the Siwa Oasis in the western Egyptian desert, where Alexander the Great was hailed as the son of the god in 331 BCE. Egyptian influence is well attested in Philistia: as a frontier staging ground and defensive buffer against invaders, Gaza in particular played a historically important role, and it is quite possible, though not certain, that parts of the Philistian coast came under Egyptian influence, or even Egyptian control, during the period of Egyptian independence from 404/399 to 343 BCE.Philistian coinage, however, drew on iconographic elements from across the eastern Mediterranean and the Levant. Its motifs should therefore not automatically be read as direct political messages or professions of allegiance, but rather as evidence of Philistia’s position at the crossroads of the north-south route between Egypt and the Fertile Crescent, the Arabian trade routes, and the Mediterranean sea lanes. Thus, in the case of the present coin, one need not necessarily assume direct iconographic influence from Egypt; it may instead point to connections with Kyrenaica, where Zeus Ammon was repeatedly depicted together with a female figure or head on coins. descripcion_anverso: ★ Unique and unpublished, and of great iconographical interest ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Philistian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Subaeratus, 14 mm, 2.34 g, 6 h). Bearded male head to right, hair gathered on the back.
descripcion_reverso: Hybrid head composed of a bearded male head to right, with a facing gorgoneion, tongue protruding, emerging from the back of the male head at a right angle; all within incuse square. Gitler & Tal -, cf. VI.4Da = Leu Judaica 32 above (for obverse) and XIII.5D and XVI.34D (for reverse). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Unique and unpublished save for its previous auction appearances. Beautifully toned and of great iconographical interest. Minor edge splits, otherwise, good very fine.From 'A very interesting collection of coins of the Jews and the Southwestern Levant', Numismatica Ars Classica 59, 4 April 2011, 1273 (with original ticket), and ex Classical Numismatic Group Mail Bid Sale 84, 5 May 2010, 741.This type, not yet recorded by Gitler & Tal 2006, is particularly important for the way in which it links several types iconographically. The reverse is already known from XIII.5D and XVI.34D, while the obverse, with its Aradian-style bearded head, recalls VI.4Da and XVII.5D–7D.In its 2011 auction commentary, NAC stated that 'several specimens of this coin-type have been sold in auctions in the past years.' This is incorrect and was presumably the result of confusion with another, more common type. The present piece remains unique to this day and, apart from its previous auction appearances, unpublished.Equally noteworthy are its unusually low weight of 2.34 g and its distinctive patina, with slight traces of silver still visible in several areas. These features suggest that the coin may originally have consisted of a silver-plated bronze core and subsequently lost most of its silver coating, leaving the bronze core exposed. If this interpretation is correct, the silver layer must have been extremely thin, as the designs remain remarkably sharp on the underlying bronze core. descripcion_anverso: ★ Unique and with a highly important overstrike ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Philistian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 11 mm, 0.71 g, 12 h). Bearded male head to right, surmounted by a long-tailed crouching lion to right with reverted head and open jaws (?).
descripcion_reverso: Hybrid janiform head, with male (?) head facing and bearded male head in profile to right, within dotted square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XVI.24Oa = Gitler, Johananoff and Tal, Overstrikes (forthcoming), Fig. 1 and Fig. 4, XVI.24Oa ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Unique and of great importance. A beautifully toned piece with intricate iconography and a fascinating overstrike. Traces of overstriking, otherwise, extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.Gitler & Tal left open whether the clearly visible head of Bes on the reverse of this unique obol formed part of the original die design, with the frontal head serving as its mouth, or whether it resulted from an overstrike. Closer examination of the surviving traces, however, allows the question to be resolved in favour of an overstrike. The slightly tilted impression of the incuse square belonging to the Bes type is clearly visible, as is its beaded neck truncation. The latter is particularly significant, since it permits the identification not only of the undertype but also of the specific die: its form is entirely characteristic of Gitler & Tal XVIII.1Oa, as may be seen especially clearly on Jeselsohn 303 and Leu Web Auction 32 (2024), 836. Gitler, Johananoff and Tal have independently arrived at the same identification and will discuss the coin as an overstrike in a forthcoming article.Traces of overstriking are likewise visible on the obverse, including an additional beaded border and a curious 'right angle' at 6 o’clock. The latter is most probably not an overstrike trace on that coin, but part of the design of the Bes die itself, having been misinterpreted as an overstrike trace on Jeselsohn 303. As the die-identical specimen in Leu Web Auction 32 (2024), 836, demonstrates, it actually belongs to the die itself, which was rather worn and may therefore have been reworked. The fact that this 'right angle' appears so low on the flan, with an additional beaded border visible above it, suggests that the undertype had been double struck, or had perhaps itself already been overstruck.This interpretation also has the advantage of making the iconography of our coin much clearer. The obverse shows a bearded head surmounted by a recumbent lion facing right, a motif also encountered on Gitler & Tal XIV.35 (cf. lots 67-70 above). The reverse, in turn, depicts a janiform head, with one face turned to the right and the other shown frontally, precisely as on the obverse of Gitler & Tal XIV.35, except that here the right-facing face is bearded. In style and execution, the coin also recalls Gitler & Tal XVIII.8 (see lots 108-109 below). We are therefore dealing with a coin of exceptionally complex iconography, whose overstriking on Gitler & Tal XVIII.1Oa also makes it of considerable technical and chronological importance. It is regrettable that the present piece is off-center on the obverse, since, in terms of condition, it is undoubtedly the finest known example from the entire series. A superb coin, with a beautifully rendered male head on the obverse and a dramatic, intensely expressive depiction of Bes on the reverse. Struck from a somewhat worn obverse die and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, nearly extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.This magnificent drachm shows on its reverse a particularly impressive representation of Bes, the ancient Egyptian protective deity. He appears in his typical frontal form, long-bearded and full-cheeked, with a bulbous nose and a plumed headdress. Here, however, the headdress is further adorned with two animal protomes turned to left and right: the one on the left may represent a horned animal, perhaps a horse or a griffin, while the one on the right is perhaps leonine. The headdress is reminiscent of the double Bes-heads with a headdress composed of two lions on Gitler & Tal XVIII.8 (see lots 102-103 below) and Gitler & Tal XXVIII.1Da (lot 118 below).Also of interest is the unusual ‘collar’ below the beard, probably a beaded broad collar of a kind encountered in ancient Egyptian art (cf. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, inv. 22.1.248). The same collar also appears on the obols (cf. lot 99 below). This detail proved particularly important in the case of lot 91 above, where it helped to identify the undertype (cf. also Haim Gitler, Mati Johananoff and Oren Tal, Bes (forthcoming)). descripcion_reverso: Double facing gorgoneion (?), consisting of an upright and an inverted face sharing a single mouth; to left, 𐡔 (Š in Aramaic); all within dotted oval border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XVIII.3Da = Gitler & Tal, Reclassifying, p. 14., Fig. 4 = Gitler, Johananoff & Tal, Bes (forthcoming), Table 1. 12. CP XVIII.3Da = Mildenberg, Petra, p. 65, 28 ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 304 ( same dies ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare and by far the finest of only two known examples – or three, if one includes Classical Numismatic Group 118 (2021), 590, a specimen overstruck with a different type. Beautifully toned and of exceptionally fine style, with a particularly impressive apotropaic reverse. Struck from a somewhat worn obverse die and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.Whether these striking grotesque faces are to be understood as Bes or as the gorgoneion remains disputed. Mildenberg argued in favour of Bes, while Gitler and Tal described the type more cautiously as a 'monster-like figure facing (Bes?)'. In the first volume of the Jeselsohn Collection, however, the authors identify it as a gorgoneion. The same reassessment can be seen in the case of Gitler and Tal XIII.5D, where the earlier, more cautious description is likewise revised in the Jeselsohn Collection to 'gorgoneion'. The wide-open mouth with protruding tongue speaks in favour of identifying the image as a gorgoneion, or rather as a double gorgoneion. The identification as Bes, however, is supported by the 𐡔 (Š in Aramaic) in the left field, which clearly connects the present piece with XVIII.1-2, on which the Egyptian protective god appears on the reverse, though without the gaping mouth and protruding tongue.As suggested in the commentary on lot 53 above, framing the question in strictly either/or terms may be too modern an approach. The image is perhaps better understood not as a case of mistaken identification, but as one of meaningful iconographic overlap: since both the gorgoneion and Bes were credited with apotropaic power, Philistine artists may here have combined features established in different visual traditions. The apotropaic force of the image was probably considered more important than strict iconographic clarity. The drachm plays on apotropaic associations: the frontal and hybrid heads evoke vigilance and warning, while the lions emphasize the fierce, protective power of Bes. In this sense, this beautiful coin almost takes on the character of a protective amulet.Also of interest is the curved line on the cheek of the right-facing head on the reverse, which appears not to have been previously commented upon. Unlike the vertical line that crosses it, this is not a die break, but a deliberate ornamental detail. It recalls the crescent on Athenian tetradrachms, from which the profile of the right-facing head also was adapted. It is therefore possible that the right-facing head, despite the shared coiffure linking it to the frontal bearded male face, is not male after all, but female – or, more likely, deliberately ambiguous, in keeping with the generally hybrid character of the coin’s wonderful imagery. Janiform head composed of a bearded male head to right and a human face to left (or facing frontally?), the latter rendered in distinctly lower relief; all within circular dotted border within shallow circular incuse.
descripcion_reverso: Lion advancing right above an ibex recumbent right, rendered in incuse outline; all within a dotted square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XIX.11Da ( this coin ). Hendin - Jeselsohn -. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Unique and of great numismatic importance. A magnificent coin, beautifully toned, with exceptional iconography and an extraordinary combination of raised relief and incuse outline engraving. The obverse struck somewhat off center, otherwise, extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.This magnificent piece is undoubtedly one of the great highlights of the Leu Judaica Collection. Its unusual combination of iconography, style, and technical execution stands out even within the remarkably inventive world of Philistian coinage.The obverse shows a janiform human head. One half is formed by a bearded male head facing right, a type familiar from numerous other Philistian coins (cf. lots 34, 64 and 104 above; the last of these is especially close to the present coin because of the lion motif). The other half, unfortunately only partly visible because of the off-center strike, shows a second human face. Unlike the bearded head, it is not rendered in high relief, but is set noticeably deeper and probably faces left, although Gitler and Tal also considered the possibility of a frontal representation. This unusual contrast between the raised bearded head and the more deeply set second face makes the janiform image particularly striking.Remarkably, a similar contrast appears on the reverse. Here, a lion advances right above a recumbent ibex, also facing right. The contrast between the two animals is expressed not only iconographically, but also technically: the lion is rendered in relief, while the ibex is shown incuse. The two sides of the coin are therefore closely connected by the same visual logic – relief against incuse, dominance against subordination, predator against prey.The motif of a lion attacking an ibex or related caprid is deeply rooted in ancient Near Eastern pictorial tradition, as illustrated, for example, by a southern Mesopotamian cylinder seal of the 13th century BCE in the Morgan Library & Museum (Morgan Seal 602). The present coin is therefore not an isolated invention, but translates a long-established pictorial scheme into an exceptional numismatic form. While the broader iconographic background is Near Eastern, the adaptation of the motif to coinage may point more directly to a Phoenician, and perhaps Sidonian, milieu. On the coinage of Sidon, caprids appear both as isolated heads and as complete animals, often rendered incuse. Particularly noteworthy are the double shekels from the time of Baʿalšillem I, circa 425-401 BCE, on which the Persian Great King is shown in a chariot above an incuse goat or ibex running left with its head turned back. Here, too, the caprid is placed beneath the dominant image and rendered in a reduced, incuse form – a striking parallel for the visual hierarchy on the present coin.The type is equally remarkable from a technical point of view. First, all three known denominations belonging to this group – the present drachm, as well as the likewise unique obol and hemiobol (Gitler & Tal XXIX.11DOa and XXIX.12DHOa) – are off-center on the obverse in a strikingly similar manner. This correspondence is unlikely to be accidental and probably reflects a technical factor. Secondly, both the present drachm and the obol display an obverse incuse. Coins with incuses on both sides are extremely unusual. Normally, the obverse die was set into an anvil, so that no incuse could be produced on that side; alternatively, the obverse die was considerably broader than the reverse die, causing the flan to bulge only over the reverse die during striking. In the present case, however, the obverse die seems to have had only a narrow border and to have been used without being deeply set into an anvil.It is this combination of unusual iconography, ancient Near Eastern pictorial tradition, and technical originality that makes the coin one of the most fascinating issues of Philistian coinage. descripcion_anverso: ★ Unique and with enigmatic iconography ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Philistian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 14 mm, 3.06 g, 12 h). Lion attacking stag to right (?).
descripcion_reverso: Male head right, wearing a headdress in the form of a lion springing right, its head turned back left toward an uncertain symbol; all within guillloche-pattern border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XIX.22Da = Gitler, Johananoff and Tal, Overstrikes, Fig. 4, XIX.22Da ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Unique and with enigmatic iconography. Rough surfaces and with two small test cuts on the reverse, otherwise, good fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.Interpreting the layered iconography of this unique piece is difficult. The obverse probably shows an animal standing right, perhaps a stag attacked from above by a lion, as found in similar form on Jeselsohn 321. Representations of this kind occur especially on coins from Kition and on issues struck under the satrap Mazaios at Tarsos.The reverse shows a bearded male head facing right, wearing a lion-shaped headdress: the lion springs right, with its head turned back to the left. In front of the lion’s head is an unusual leaf-shaped symbol with a stem and what may be an eye. Gitler and Tal suggest a calf’s head, but this identification remains uncertain. Unfortunately, the details are difficult to discern because of corrosion and horn silver deposits, so that misinterpretations remain possible.The description of the reverse border as 'dotted' should be corrected: it is in fact rendered as a guilloche-pattern border. Furthermore, only one foreleg of the lion is shown; the supposed left foreleg indicated by Gitler and Tal in their drawing is most likely merely an accretion of horn silver.Iconographically, the lion-shaped headdress clearly links this piece to Gitler & Tal XXIX.20, as well as to lots 67-70 and 91 above: in each case, the human head or heads are crowned by leonine figures, a striking and highly unusual motif within the Philistian issues. Somewhat rough and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.The obverse of this impressive drachm recalls lots 66 and 100 above. Here too, the head appears to be wearing a helmet, decorated with a laurel wreath as on lot 66. The reverse, on the other hand, harkens back to the coinage of Kelenderis in Cilicia, whose coat of arms was a kneeling he-goat. A charming detail in the rendering of the he-goat, or ibex, as Gitler & Tal call it, is the appearance of an owl's head concealed on its right shoulder - another reference to the Athenian silver coinage that dominated international trade in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. Good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003, and from the Jascha Heifetz Collection, Part II, Superior Galleries, 9-10 December 1989, 2792.Jascha Heifetz (1901-1987), born in Vilnius, was one of the most celebrated violinists of the 20th century and set standards of technical perfection that profoundly influenced generations of musicians. After leaving Russia with his family, he made his sensational American debut at Carnegie Hall in 1917 and became a U.S. citizen in 1925, eventually settling in Los Angeles.Beyond music, Heifetz was a passionate and discerning collector, with interests ranging from rare books and stamps to coins. His involvement with numismatics extended over many decades, with coins from his collection already appearing at auction in the 1930s. Following his death in 1987, his extensive coin collection was offered by Superior Galleries in two major sales in 1989, encompassing American, ancient and world coins. descripcion_anverso: ★ Extremely rare and of great interest ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Philistian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 10 mm, 0.61 g, 6 h). Bearded male head to left, three-quarter facing, hair gathered at the back.
descripcion_reverso: Nude youth, holding whip, seated sideways on a galloping horse and preparing to dismount, perhaps performing the kalpé; all within dotted square within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XXV.3Oa = YC p. 128, Fig. VI.1 ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare and of great interest. Slightly rough and struck from a somewhat worn reverse die, otherwise, good very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.For the obverse, one may compare a remarkable bulla from Carthage, illustrated by Gitler & Tal on pl. LIV, Fig. 4.7, which shows an almost identical head in three-quarter view (cf. also lots 58-59 and 97 above). The reverse, however, should probably be understood differently: it does not show a rider holding back a passing horse, but rather a youth seated sideways on the horse and about to dismount. On the two specimens known to Gitler & Tal, including the present piece, the details were difficult to discern because of the break in the reverse die. The specimen offered in Triton XXVI (2023), 399, on which the die break is less advanced, clearly shows that the rider is seated sideways on the horse.The scene probably represents the kalpé (Greek καλπή), a race for mares in which the riders dismounted during the final part of the race and ran beside the animals to the finish, holding the bridle or reins (P. Veselý, The Dismounting Horseman Scene on Cilician Coins, in: KOINON 6, 2023, pp. 20–50). Comparable depictions are known from various Greek cities, especially Himera and Gela in Sicily, as well as Holmoi and, above all, Kelenderis in Cilicia, the likeliest source of the iconographic influence on the Philistian issue.According to Pausanias, the kalpe was introduced as an Olympic event in the 71st Olympiad (= 496 BC), but was abolished in the 84th Olympiad (= 444 BC) (Pausanias 5.9.1–2). Beyond its agonistic character, the race probably also had a military dimension, since it trained skills relevant to the equestrian and military training of young citizens. descripcion_anverso: ★ An extremely rare moschophoros ('calf-bearer') Rbʾ Šql ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Philistian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 15 mm, 3.56 g, 3 h). Bearded male head to right within circular guilloche-pattern border.
descripcion_reverso: Man standing right, carrying a recumbent calf right across his shoulders and placing his right hand on the back of another calf walking right, an owl concealed within the latter’s body; before, branch; all within square guilloche-pattern border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XXVI.1Db ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Mildenberg, Imagery, pl. III, 53 ( same dies ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare. Attractively toned and with a very interesting reverse. The obverse struck somewhat off center and with the usual test cut on the reverse, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.Gitler & Tal describe the figure on the reverse as a moschophoros, or calf-bearer, a figure belonging to the broader tradition of animal-bearers in ancient art. The most famous example of this type is the so-called ‘Calf-Bearer’ from Athens, an archaic statue of circa 570–560 BCE showing a man carrying a calf on his shoulders as an offering to Athena. The animal at the calf-bearer’s feet on the present coin, however, is interpreted by Gitler & Tal as a dog. Yet the close resemblance between the head of the calf carried on the shoulders and the head of the supposed ‘dog’ strongly suggests that the animal at the figure’s feet is also a calf rather than a dog (see also the piece sold in Classical Numismatic Group 120, 2022, 481).If the animal at the figure’s feet is indeed a second calf rather than a dog, the scene takes on a more explicitly sacrificial character: it would show a figure bringing or presenting calves for sacrifice. While rooted in the broader Eastern Mediterranean tradition of animal-offering imagery, the motif also resonates in the southern Levant, where cattle, especially calves and bulls, played an important role in sacrificial practice, as reflected, for example, in biblical texts. This makes the type a particularly interesting Philistian adaptation of a widely recognizable sacrificial image. descripcion_anverso: ★ The most detailed depiction of the Achaemenid-inspired horned lion-griffin on Philistian coinage ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Philistian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 15 mm, 3.61 g, 6 h). Youthful female head to right, hair gathered at the back.
descripcion_reverso: Head of a horned lion-griffin right, horns terminating in duck heads, devouring a horse protome; all within dotted square border within incuse square. BMC Palestine pl. XIX, 23 ( same dies ). Gitler & Tal XXVII.6Db ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 351 ( same dies ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Extremely rare and among the finest of a very few known examples. A very interesting piece with a highly attractive reverse. The obverse struck from a somewhat worn die and with two test cuts on the reverse edge, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.This wonderful piece offers what is probably the most detailed depiction of the Achaemenid-inspired horned lion-griffin on Philistian coinage. By reducing the full figure to a single head, the engraver gives the image remarkable focus: not only the powerfully rendered, almost savage lion’s head is visible, but also the finely ribbed horns, which terminate in duck heads. With jaws wide open, the lion-griffin devours its prey, a horse shown only as a protome.In condensing a classic animal-combat scene, familiar from many ancient coin types, into so compact an image, the artist created a composition of striking intensity and beauty. Comparisons may be drawn with the lion and bull at Akanthos (cf. also lot 36 above), or with the lion and stag at Velia, Tarsos, and Kition. At the same time, the image reflects not only the broad cultural currents of the Levantine world, but also a distinctly local Philistian adaptation of them.
