descripcion_anverso: ★ Of the highest rarity, one of just two known examples, and with highly interesting iconographic hierarchy ★ PHILISTIA. Central Mint. Philistian-styled, circa 420-350 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 17 mm, 3.54 g, 4 h). Facing head of Bes, wearing long beard and plumed headdress, flanked by two upright lions with heads turned back; below, four-row beaded collar.
descripcion_reverso: Lion recumbent right, head facing, above gazelle prostrate to right; all within dotted square border within incuse square. Gitler & Tal XXVIII.1Da ( this coin ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn 355 ( same dies ). Mildenberg, Palästina, pl. LVIII, 72 ( this coin ). Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Of the highest rarity, one of just two known examples. Somewhat rough and with a test cut on the reverse, otherwise, very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.As an apotropaic deity, Bes often appears in grotesque and fearsome form, his wild appearance serving to ward off evil. This is also where his close association with the lion comes into play: the animal’s strength and threatening presence further enhance the god’s protective power. On the present piece, the two lions flanking the headdress therefore intensify Bes’ apotropaic character. At the same time, the composition emphasizes his command over the animal world. On a scarab seal in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, probably Phoenician and dating to the 6th–5th century BCE (41.160.163), Bes is likewise shown standing between two lions, restraining them with his arms; compare also lot 120 below. Bes thus not only wards off evil, but also appears as master of animals.The same hierarchy of power is continued on the reverse, where a lion appears in a dominant pose above a gazelle. Bes, the apotropaic demon, commands the lions; the lion, in turn, dominates the gazelle. The two sides of the coin thus form a clear hierarchy of power, moving from supernatural protective power to the ruler of the animal world and finally to the herbivore as prey. Particularly striking is the lion’s frontal face, which once again underscores the apotropaic character of the coin. descripcion_anverso: ★ Perhaps the earliest Samarian coinage, by a governor known from the Book of Nehemiah ★ SAMARIA. Series with personal names and miscellaneous letters. Sanballat (?), governor of Samaria, circa 430-407 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 16 mm, 3.20 g, 1 h). Two male figures in close combat: at left, a dominant figure standing right, grasping his opponent by the hair and pressing a dagger (?) to his throat; at right, his opponent giving way to left, right leg slightly bent, left leg deeply flexed, both arms extended in defence; between them, 𐡎𐡁 (SB in Aramaic); all within dotted square border.
descripcion_reverso: Two bearded soldiers standing face to face, each holding spear and round shield; the left figure with a quiver (?) on his back; the right figure rendered incuse except for the shield boss, which is decorated with a facing head of Bes in relief; all within incuse square. CSC 71 = Samuels, Rynearson & Meshorer 24 = Shoshana I 20059 = Wyssmann p. 259, MQ 49.a ( same dies ). Hendin -. Jeselsohn -. Meshorer & Qedar 49 ( same dies ). Sofaer -. Extremely rare and of great historical interest. Large test cut and some cleaning scratches, otherwise, nearly very fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.This highly important coin forms part of the so-called Sanballat group of Samarian coinage. The point of departure for this group is the Aramaic legend 𐡎𐡁, SB, long associated with Sanballat, one of the few historically well-attested officials of Persian-period Samaria. Sanballat, called 'the Horonite' in the biblical tradition, is best dated, in the narrower framework of recent scholarship, to about 430-407 BCE, when he appears to have served as governor of Samaria. He is known above all from the Book of Nehemiah, where he emerges as the principal opponent of Nehemiah, a Jewish official at the Persian court who came to Jerusalem with royal authorization to strengthen the city’s political and defensive position. Already Nehemiah’s arrival 'displeased them greatly' (Neh. 2:10), and Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem responded to the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s wall with the pointed question: 'Are you rebelling against the king?' (Neh. 2:19). The conflict is therefore best understood not as a matter of personal or religious hostility, but as one of regional power politics: a fortified Jerusalem strengthened Yehud and could diminish Samaria’s influence.The most important extra-biblical testimony for Sanballat’s historical existence is the Elephantine letter of 407 BCE, which explicitly refers to 'Delayah and Shelemyah, the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria' (TAD A4.7 and lot 125 below). This confirms Sanballat’s office independently of Nehemiah and shows that his sons Delayah and Shelemiah were already politically relevant figures in 407 BCE. Sanballat thus appears not as an isolated adversary of Jerusalem, but as the head of a Samarian elite family whose next generation becomes historically visible in Delayah and Shelemiah.The attribution of the coins to Sanballat himself remains unproven, but their late 5th-century BCE date is technically and iconographically convincing. Of particular interest is the scene on the obverse of the present coin, depicting two male figures in close combat. The dominant figure on the left seizes his opponent by the hair and holds a dagger (?) to his throat. The meaning of the scene is not entirely clear, but it recalls representations of the Great King on Sidonian coins and on Samarian issues of Sidonian type (CSC, pp. 257 ff.), although in these depictions the king grasps a lion by the mane. For the reverse, see the commentary under lot 123 below. descripcion_anverso: ★ Sanballat (?), governor of Samaria, and ex Leu 75, 25 October 1999, 1323 ★ SAMARIA. Series with personal names and miscellaneous letters. Sanballat (?), governor of Samaria, circa 430-407 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 9 mm, 0.70 g, 12 h). Two bearded (?) soldiers standing face to face, each holding spear and round shield; all within a dotted square border.
descripcion_reverso: Two bearded soldiers standing face to face, each holding spear and round shield; the right figure rendered incuse except for the shield boss, which is in relief; all within incuse square. CSC 72. Hendin -. Jeselsohn 76-78. Meshorer & Qedar 50. NH -. Samuels, Rynearson & Meshorer, Legacy, 25. Shoshana I 20041 = Sofaer 163. Wyssmann p. 260, MQ 50. Very rare and among the finest known examples. Beautifully toned and very well centered. About extremely fine.Ex Leu 75, 25 October 1999, 1323 (with original ticket).Although anepigraphic, the present type may be placed, on account of its close iconographic relationship with CSC 71, within the orbit of the so-called Sanballat group of Samarian coinage (see lot 122 above and 124 below). A proper understanding of its imagery is therefore important. In the earlier auction commentary on this coin in Leu 75 (1999), 1323, it was suggested that 'the differing headdresses worn by the two soldiers on the obverse of this small coin clearly indicate that one is a Persian while the other is probably a Greek mercenary […]'. Although interesting, this interpretation is ultimately untenable. It presupposes a Persian–Greek contrast for which the coin itself provides no evidence and turns an uncertain observation concerning the shape of the head into an ethnic identification.Comparison with other specimens argues against this interpretation, and the supposed helmet worn by the soldier on the right is no more than an optical illusion (cf. CSC 72a–b). The reverse, too, evidently repeats the same motif as the obverse, albeit in a charming incuse adaptation, with the shield rendered in relief; on the drachm in lot 121 above, the shield is instead rendered as a facing head of Bes. Both figures are bearded and similarly armed. The figure on the left on the reverse lacks a shield, although he may be carrying a quiver over his shoulder. In both their appearance and equipment, the figures are far more closely comparable to Persian guards than to a scene contrasting a Persian soldier with a Greek mercenary.The closest numismatic parallel occurs on staters from Tarsos dating to the second half of the fifth century BCE, on which two spearmen equipped with quivers face one another (Traité II.2, pl. CVI, 6). It is entirely conceivable that the present type was directly inspired by these Cilician models, although both ultimately draw upon the visual repertoire of imperial Achaemenid art. The closest iconographic parallels are provided by the Persian guards depicted on the Apadana stairway at Persepolis, where bearded soldiers shown in profile carry spears and round or rounded shields with central bosses, sometimes arranged in opposing groups.The present type is therefore best understood not as depicting a Persian confronting a Greek mercenary, but as a local Samarian adaptation of an Achaemenid military motif, firmly rooted in the visual language of the Achaemenid Empire. descripcion_anverso: ★ The finest known Rbʾ Šql of Delayah (?), son of Sanballat ★ SAMARIA. Series with personal names and miscellaneous letters. Delayah (?), governor of Samaria, circa 407-380/70 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 14 mm, 4.20 g, 6 h). Bridled horse standing left; in upper right field, 𐡃 or 𐡓 (D or R in Aramaic); all within square guilloche-pattern border.
descripcion_reverso: Bearded, royal-headed winged sphinx seated to left; in upper right field, 𐡃 or 𐡓 (D or R in Aramaic); all within square guilloche-pattern border within incuse square. CSC 87a ( this coin ). Hendin 6035 ( same dies ). Jeselsohn 40 ( same dies ). Meshorer & Qedar 28 = Sofaer 116 ( same dies ). NH -. Shoshana -. Wyssmann p. 253, MQ 28. Extremely rare and the finest known example. Boldly struck, beautifully toned and with excellent detail. Small die break on the obverse, otherwise, good extremely fine.Ex UBS 52, 11 September 2001, 125 (with original auction flip).This remarkable drachm belongs to a series of Samarian coins bearing the legend D/RY or D/R, the reading being complicated by the difficult distinction between 𐡃 and 𐡓. Eshel read the legend as DY and associated it with Delayah, a son of Sanballat known from the Aramaic Elephantine papyri; Sanballat was the Persian-period governor of Samaria (Eshel 2007, pp. 228-229, see also lots 122-124 above). Delayah, written in Aramaic as 𐡃𐡋𐡉𐡄, appears there in a specific political context. When the Jewish military colony at Elephantine in Egypt sought permission to rebuild its temple of YHW (Yahweh) after its destruction, it addressed its appeal in 407 BCE not only to Bagohi, governor of Judah, but also to 'Delayah and Shelemyah, the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria' (TAD A4.7). Delayah’s standing is made still clearer by the related memorandum TAD A4.9, which opens: 'Memorandum of what Bagohi and Delayah said.' Delayah thus appears alongside the Judean governor as an authority whose approval or recommendation carried weight in the affairs of the Elephantine community.The identification of the coin legend with this Delayah remains a numismatic hypothesis (for a coin tentatively assigned to his brother Shelemyah, see lot 129 below), but it is historically plausible. The Sanballat family is one of the few Samarian elites of the late fifth and early fourth centuries BCE documented in both literary and epigraphic sources. Sanballat himself is known from Nehemiah as 'the Horonite' and is explicitly described in the Elephantine papyri as governor of Samaria (see lot 122 above). The fact that his sons Delayah and Shelemyah appear as addressees in 407 BCE suggests that they were already involved in the administration, perhaps acting on behalf of their aging father or preparing for succession in office.A further, though fragmentary, piece of evidence comes from the Wadi Daliyeh finds. Bulla WD 22 has been plausibly reconstructed by Jan Dušek as the seal of a Delayah/Delayahu, son of Sanballat, governor of Samaria. Since the inscription is damaged, this cannot be presented as certain proof; nevertheless, the proposed reading fits remarkably well with the Elephantine evidence. Delayah is therefore often understood in scholarship as the presumed successor of Sanballat in the governorship of Samaria, with a period of activity extending roughly from 407 BCE into the early fourth century BCE.If the legend of the present drachm is indeed to be connected with Delayah, the coin would not be merely an anonymous local issue of Samaria. It would belong to the milieu of a historically identifiable governor’s family whose names stand at the intersection of biblical tradition, Aramaic administrative practice, Persian provincial politics, and Samarian coinage. This is what makes the series so compelling: our coins (lots 125-128) may preserve a name that becomes tangible within the major political and religious tensions of the late Achaemenid period, from Jerusalem and Samaria to Elephantine on the southern Nile. descripcion_anverso: ★ Extremely rare and in exceptional condition for the issue ★ SAMARIA. Series with personal names and miscellaneous letters. Delayah (?), governor of Samaria, circa 407-380/70 BCE. Rbʾ Šql = Drachm (Silver, 14 mm, 4.05 g, 4 h). Bridled horse standing left, forelock tied up with a ribbon into an upright tuft; in upper right field, 𐡃 or 𐡓 (D or R in Aramaic); all within square guilloche-pattern border.
descripcion_reverso: Bearded, royal-headed winged sphinx seated to left; in upper right field, 𐡃 or 𐡓 (D or R in Aramaic); all within square guilloche-pattern border within incuse square. CSC 87. Hendin 6035 ( same dies ). Jeselsohn 40 ( same dies ). Meshorer & Qedar 28 = Sofaer 116 ( same dies ). NH -. Shoshana -. Wyssmann p. 253, MQ 28. Extremely rare and in exceptional condition for the issue. Beautifully toned and with fully struck inscriptions. Extremely fine.From the collection of Alan Irvin Casden, privately acquired from him in 2003.For a fuller discussion of the possible attribution of this series to Delayah, see the commentary to lot 125 above. On the present piece, the two letters on both obverse and reverse are exceptionally clear; their broad form favours a reading as 𐡃 rather than 𐡓, and thus supports the attribution to Delayah. The appeal of the type, however, is not only historical but also iconographic. Like many Philistian and Samarian issues, it draws freely on Achaemenid visual language. The horse appears to wear a stylized tied forelock (cf. lot 36 above), a feature well known from Persian representations of horses. The reverse shows a sphinx with a bearded, crowned, royal-type head, evoking the Persian Great King. Very close parallels, though with the heads turned backwards, are preserved on the famous glazed-brick panels with opposed sphinxes from the palace of Dareios I at Susa, now in the Louvre (Louvre Sb 3325). The coins thus condense the political and artistic world of Achaemenid Samaria: local authority expressed through the language of imperial imagery. (owl not mentioned). Very rare. Beautifully toned and very well centered for the issue. Like Delayah, Shelemyah is mentioned in one of the Aramaic papyri from Elephantine: 'Delayah and Shelemyah, the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria' (cf. TAD A4.7 and lots 128 and 131 above).Unlike his brother, however, Shelemyah does not appear in TAD A4.9, where Delayah is mentioned alongside Bagohi, the governor of Judah. This may suggest that Shelemyah occupied a less prominent position and that Delayah alone served as governor of Samaria. If the attribution of the coins to the family of Sanballat is correct, however, another possibility is that Shelemyah either succeeded his brother as governor or preceded him in office. descripcion_anverso: ★ An exceptionally well preserved Mʿh of Pharnabazos, Achaemenid commander for the Egyptian campaign ★ SAMARIA. Series with place names and related types. Pharnabazos, Achaemenid commander for the Egyptian campaign, circa 380-373 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 9 mm, 0.75 g, 12 h). Youthful male head to left, wearing Phrygian cap bound with a taenia knotted above the forehead; to right, CAꓭ𐤫ꟼAΦ.
descripcion_reverso: Forepart of Pegasos to right; below, 𐡔𐡓𐡌𐡍 (ŠMRN in retrograde Aramaic); all within shallow circular incuse. CSC 39. Meshorer & Qedar 1. Hendin -. Jeselsohn 1-3. NH -. Shoshana -. Sofaer 44. Wyssmann p. 243, MQ 1. Very rare and exceptionally well preserved, struck on a broad flan and with beautiful toning. Very likely the finest known example. Light die wear, otherwise, extremely fine.Ex UBS 52, 11 September 2001, 123 (with original auction flip).The precise connection between Pharnabazos and Samaria remains unclear. Pharnabazos was the long-serving satrap of Daskylitis, or Hellespontine Phrygia, and played an important role in the final years of the Peloponnesian War and the subsequent struggle against Sparta. His career reached one of its high points in 394 BCE, when the Persian fleet under Pharnabazos and the Athenian admiral Konon defeated the Spartans at Knidos. Later, Artaxerxes II entrusted him with the reconquest of rebellious Egypt. From about 380 BCE, Pharnabazos was active in the Cilician-Syrian region, where a substantial coinage was struck in his name, especially at Tarsos, probably to help finance and prepare the Egyptian expedition.After several years of preparation, Pharnabazos led a large Persian expeditionary force from his base at Ake in southern Phoenicia to Egypt in 373 BCE. The campaign at first met with some success in the Nile Delta, but it ultimately failed in the face of Egyptian resistance, Persian delays, and the rising Nile flood, which forced the army to withdraw. Pharnabazos disappears from the historical record after this failure, and the date of his death is unknown. In this context, a date of circa 380-373 BCE for the Samarian coins in his name seems plausible. It is possible that they were struck in 373 BCE, when Pharnabazos assembled his troops at Ake, not far from Samaria, but this cannot be proven. descripcion_anverso: ★ Very rare exceptionally well preserved for this interesting issue ★ SAMARIA. Series with place names and related types. Mazaios, satrap of Cilicia, 361/0-333 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 10 mm, 0.54 g, 6 h), circa 353-333. Biga galloping right, driven by a male figure wearing a Persian headdress, holding goad in his right hand and reins in his left; behind him, a similar, but bearded figure standing right, raising his right hand.
descripcion_reverso: Persian Great King or hero standing right, confronting a lion and grasping it by the mane; between them, 𐡌𐡆 (MZ in Aramaic); all within incuse square. CSC 22. Hendin -. Jeselsohn 124. Meshorer & Qedar 74 = Wyssmann p. 268, MQ 74.d ( this coin ). NH -. Shoshana -. Sofaer -. Very rare. Beautifully toned and exceptionally well preserved for this interesting issue. Minor roughness on the obverse, otherwise, extremely fine.Ex UBS 52, 11 September 2001, 126 (with original auction flip), and previously from the Gil Chaya Collection.Mazaios was a high-ranking Achaemenid official of the fourth century BCE and is best known as satrap of Cilicia, where he issued an extensive coinage at Tarsos. His Cilician coinage is usually dated to around 361/0-333 BCE. In the course of his career, his authority appears to have extended beyond Cilicia to Syria and Eber-Nari, the territory 'Beyond the River.' In the final years of the Achaemenid Empire, under Dareios III, he was one of the most important Persian commanders in the war against Alexander 'the Great' and the Macedonians. At the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE, he fought on the Persian side against Alexander. After the Persian defeat, he surrendered Babylon to Alexander without resistance, and Alexander subsequently confirmed him as satrap of Babylonia. Mazaios probably died in 328 BCE while still holding this office.The present coin was classified in CSC under place names rather than personal names in order to group it with the other two obols of Mazaios, both of which bear the Samarian ethnic. We follow this arrangement here, although it is somewhat misleading. The Samarian coinage associated with Mazaios is iconographically closely related to his Sidonian issues, whose dated series fall within the years 353-333 BCE. The Samarian coins should therefore probably be placed in the same period. descripcion_anverso: ★ The enigmatic Jeroboam ★ SAMARIA. Series with personal names and miscellaneous letters. Jeroboam, circa mid 4th century BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 10 mm, 0.45 g, 11 h). Satrap seated right on diphros, wearing Persian dress and testing arrow; to right, 𐡉𐡓𐡁𐡏𐡌 (YRBʿM in Aramaic).
descripcion_reverso: Two female figures with long hair and pleated robes standing opposite one another; the figure on the left raises her right hand to her mouth, while the figure on the right holds an indistinct object in her right hand; both within a flat-roofed rectangular shrine shown in left half-perspective, its visible left exterior wall decorated with a horizontal palm frond; all within a circular incuse. CSC 153. Hendin -. Jeselsohn 71. Meshorer & Qedar 45. NH -. Shoshana -. Sofaer 103. Wyssmann p. 259, MQ 45.l ( this coin ). Very rare and nicely toned. Very fine.Ex Waddell E-Auction, 6 August 2003, 82, inv. no. 40185 (with original ticket).Apart from his coins, Jeroboam remains historically elusive. The name is Hebrew and is attested in the Israelite-Jewish onomasticon from the early first millennium BCE onward. Its interpretation is disputed: proposed meanings include 'the people contend,' 'the people multiply,' or, if ʿAm is understood not as 'people' but as a divine name, 'ʿAm fights for us.'Gitler, Johananoff, and Tal date the Jeroboam in question to the period after 353 BCE on the basis of the so-called profile eyes on some of his coins. Stylistic dating, however, is always problematic, especially when it is used with such precision and tied to Attic coinage, whose own chronology is not always secure. Nevertheless, the iconography of Jeroboam’s coins offers several important clues. Most relevant for the present coin is its close connection with the coinage of Datames, the Achaemenid satrap of Cilicia and Cappadocia (384-361/0 BCE): the satrap examining an arrow on our coin is borrowed from a stater from Tarsos of Datames belonging to Casabonne Series 2. This connection is further supported by CSC 152, which adopts the reverse type of Datames’ staters belonging to Casabonne Series 3.A broad dating of Jeroboam to the middle of the fourth century BCE therefore appears plausible; a somewhat earlier date, perhaps in the second quarter of the fourth century BCE, should also be considered possible. descripcion_anverso: ★ An exceptional Mʿh of Brochubelos, Achaemenid official in Syria in circa 345-332 BCE. ★ SAMARIA. Series with personal names and miscellaneous letters. Brochubelos, Achaemenid official in Syria, circa 345-332 BCE. Mʿh = Obol (Silver, 9 mm, 0.47 g, 12 h). Biga galloping left, driven by a male figure wearing a Persian headdress, holding goad in his right hand and reins in his left; behind him, a similar figure standing left, raising his right hand.
descripcion_reverso: Horseman galloping left, wearing Persian headdress, holding goad in right hand and reins in left; below, 𐡁𐡓𐡅𐡇𐡁𐡋 (BRWḤBL in Aramaic). CSC 163. Hendin -. Jeselsohn 24. Meshorer & Qedar 15. NH 413-419. Samuels, Rynearson & Meshorer 26 = Shoshana I 20053. Sofaer 93. Wyssmann p. 248, MQ 15. Very rare and undoubtedly among the finest known examples of this historically important series. Beautifully toned and with excellent detail. Good extremely fine.Ex UBS 52, 11 September 2001, 124 (with original auction flip).Brochubelos is known from only two brief historical references. Arrian records that in 330 BCE Antibelos, a son of Mazaios, came to Alexander 'the Great' together with the Babylonian Bagistanes and reported that Dareios III had been seized by Nabarzanes, Bessos, and Barsaentes (Arr. Anab. 3.21.1). This Antibelos is probably the same man whom Curtius Rufus, in his account of the same episode, calls Brochubelos, son of Mazaios, formerly 'praetor' of Syria ( Syriae quondam praetor, Curt. 5.13.11). Curtius is evidently using the Latin term to denote a high administrative office in Achaemenid Syria, within the wider province of Eber-Nari, which may explain why coins were issued in Brochubelos’ name at Samaria.Arrian’s Antibelos is probably a distorted Greek form of Brochubelos/Brocubelus, itself apparently a Semitic name usually understood as 'blessed by Bel.' The currently preferred reading of the Samarian coin legend as BRWḤBL further supports the identification with Brochubelos. The iconography of this remarkable obol, however, remains difficult to interpret. Gitler, Johananoff, and Tal relate the chariot scene to Sidonian coin types, where the charioteer and the Great King are clearly distinguished. On the Samarian coins, by contrast, the two figures in the chariot are dressed almost identically, as is the horseman on the reverse. It therefore remains unclear whether the scene shows Brochubelos with the Great King, Brochubelos with a charioteer, or the Great King with his charioteer. descripcion_anverso: ★ The exceptional depiction of five Athenian-style coins on a coin ★ SAMARIA. Anepigraphic types with Achaemenid and regional influences. Circa 400-332 BCE. Half Mʿh = Hemiobol (Silver, 7 mm, 0.23 g, 12 h). Janiform bearded male head.
descripcion_reverso: Five Athenian-style coins with owls in a flower-like arrangement. CSC 206. Hendin -. Jeselsohn 246. Gitler, Johananoff, Lichtenberger & Tal, Reflexivity, pl. 2, 18 = Meshorer & Qedar pl. 21, 142 ( this coin ) = Wyssmann p. 291, MQ 142f. ( this coin ). NH -. Shoshana -. Sofaer 186. Very rare and in exceptional condition for the issue, perhaps the finest known example. Beautifully toned, with the owls on the reverse unusually sharp and well defined. Very minor area of weakness on the obverse, otherwise, about extremely fine.Ex UBS 52, 11 September 2001, 127 (with original auction flip), and previously from the Gil Chaya Collection.This extraordinary issue is apparently unique among ancient coin types in depicting recognizable coins as its principal reverse design, apart from more schematic representations on Roman coins, where money sometimes appears as small pellets poured by Liberalitas from a cornucopiae or as heaps at the feet of Moneta. The reverse shows five owl-type silver coins arranged in a small flower-like pile. Although the image clearly evokes the famous Athenian owl, the coins need not be understood as actual Athenian tetradrachms: in the southern Levant, owl types in the Athenian tradition were widely adopted and adapted, and large denominations on the Attic standard could be understood locally as shekels (see lots 150-151 below). The type also invites comparison with the modern Greek one-euro coin, which likewise reproduces the owl motif of the classical Athenian tetradrachm.In his article 'Coinage for Redeeming the Firstborn: an Ancient and Modern Jewish Ritual,' The Celator, December 2002, pp. 14-22, Ronn Berrol suggested that the striking number five may allude to the Pidyon ha-Ben ceremony. Pidyon ha-Ben, Hebrew for 'redemption of the son,' is the Jewish rite by which a firstborn male child is redeemed through a payment to a Kohen, a member of the priestly line. The religious basis for the rite lies in the biblical notion that the firstborn belongs in a special sense to God. In the words of the Authorized Version, Ex 13:2 states: 'Sanctify unto me all the firstborn, whatsoever openeth the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and of beast: it is mine.' The monetary aspect is made explicit in Num 18:15-16: 'nevertheless the firstborn of man shalt thou surely redeem,' and those to be redeemed 'from a month old' are to be redeemed 'for the money of five shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary.' Num 3:47-48 similarly prescribes 'five shekels apiece' and orders that the redemption money be given 'unto Aaron and to his sons.'Berrol’s interpretation is therefore highly attractive: the reverse does not merely show money, but precisely five silver coins – the same number as the five silver shekels prescribed in the biblical tradition for the redemption of the firstborn. The Samaritan-Levantine context of the issue is also significant, since Jews and Samaritans alike were bound to Pentateuchal traditions in which the sanctification and redemption of the firstborn were deeply rooted. Nor does the use of the owl type weaken the argument. In the fourth-century Levant, the Athenian owl had long since become more than a specifically Athenian civic badge: it was a widely understood monetary image, capable of being translated into local coinages and local weight denominations.Nevertheless, the interpretation must remain cautious. The coin bears no inscription explicitly referring to the firstborn, to a Kohen, to Aaron, or to the act of redemption, and the five coins cannot be identified securely as the 'five shekels' of the biblical text. The number five may therefore have carried a religious meaning, but it could equally allude to a treasure, a payment, commerce, tribute, or the special authority of owl-type silver in the eastern Mediterranean. It is precisely this ambiguity that makes the type so fascinating: the reverse shows coins on a coin – and perhaps even money as the medium of a specific religious act. (reading of the countermark) (with original ticket).In 2006, Gitler and Tal expressed serious doubts about the attribution of the countermark on V.7Ta to Gaza, although this reservation was not repeated in their 2024 publication of the Jeselsohn Collection. In the NAC commentary on the present piece – which follows that of Gitler and Tal very closely – it is suggested that the coin is probably of Attic origin ('very likely but not certainly of Athenian mintage'). Various readings have been proposed for this and related countermarks, including Gaza, but the reading and significance of the mark must ultimately remain open. descripcion_anverso: ★ An extremely rare and unusual Levantine imitation ★ SOUTHERN LEVANT. Athenian-styled Imitations. Circa 420-405 BCE or slightly later. Šql = Tetradrachm (Silver, 25 mm, 16.54 g, 9 h). Head of Athena to right, wearing crested Attic helmet decorated with three olive leaves and palmette, circular earring and necklace; before, detached lock of hair of Athena in the form of a crescent; on cheek, countermark: 𐩫 (?) (K in South Arabian) within incuse square.
descripcion_reverso: Owl standing right, head facing; to left, olive sprig and crescent; to right, Α ☉Ε; all within incuse square. Classical Numismatic Group MBS 78 (2008), 625 = Freeman & Sear MBS 14 (2007), 212 = Numismatica Ars Classica February Sale 2026, 487. Extremely rare and very unusual. Nicely toned and of lovely imitative style. Slightly rough, otherwise, good very fine.Ex UBS 49, 11 September 2000, 240 corr. (as 'Gaza?') (with original auction flip).L. Gentelli, G. Davis, F. Albarède, J. Blichert-Toff, and H. Gitler have shown in a newly published article that the majority of the supposedly local imitations of Athenian tetradrachms found in the Levant, and for that reason often attributed to Philistine workshops, are in fact official Athenian issues (When is an owl not an owl? An analysis of Attic tetradrachms circulating in the southern Levant in the late fifth and fourth centuries BCE, in: JAS Reports 70 (2026), pp. 1-11).Although the present piece can hardly be assigned to Gaza, as proposed by UBS, it is nevertheless certainly not an official issue of Athens: it is difficult to imagine an Attic die-cutter rendering Athena’s lock of hair as a crescent detached from the head and floating freely in the field. That this was not an isolated mistake is shown by the comparison piece first offered by Freeman & Sear in 2007, which displays the same detached 'crescent' but was struck from a different pair of dies. Evidently, the die-cutter or die-cutters misunderstood Athena’s lock of hair as the crescent that regularly appears beside the owl on the reverse.Where exactly these coins were produced remains unclear, but they are certainly of eastern, non-Athenian origin, most likely from the southern Levant. The countermark was interpreted by UBS as 𐡕 (T in Aramaic), though 𐩫 (K in South Arabian) is also conceivable. In any case, the countermark does not prove the coin’s place of manufacture, but rather points to its later circulation or use. descripcion_anverso: ★ Among the finest known depictions of the Ear (of God?) ★ JUDAEA, Achaemenid Province (Yehud). Circa 350-333 BCE. Half Grh = Hemiobol (Silver, 7 mm, 0.27 g, 6 h). Ear (of God?).
descripcion_reverso: [ 𐤉𐤄𐤃 ] (YHD in retrograde Paleo-Hebrew) Falcon flying upward, head to right. Hendin 6060 ( same dies ). Jeselsohn 53-54 ( same dies ). Meshorer, AJC -. Shoshana -. Sofaer YC 13 (O1/R1). Very rare and exceptionally well preserved, with a wonderfully rendered Ear (of God?), and undoubtedly among the finest known examples. The usual light die wear and struck slighly off center, otherwise, nearly extremely fine.Ex The New York Sale XLVIII, 14 January 2020, 21 (with original ticket), and previously privately acquired from Steve Rubinger on 2 January 2009 (Antiqua, with original ticket).The highly distinctive obverse of this celebrated Yehud issue presents a human ear as an independent coin type – an image apparently without parallel in ancient numismatics. Gerson connected it with the Shema, 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one' (Deut. 6:4), the foundational biblical proclamation of Israel’s monotheistic faith. Yet even more direct resonances occur in prayers asking the Lord to 'incline Your ear and hear' (2 Kgs 19:16; Isa. 37:17; Ps. 17:6; 71:2; 86:1), while Psalm 94:9 asks, 'He who planted the ear, does He not hear?'Read in this light, the image evokes the 'ear of God' – the unseen deity attentively receiving the prayers of His people. The isolated ear thus becomes a powerful visual surrogate for divine presence, translating biblical language into an image without portraying God in fully anthropomorphic form.Individual human sense organs were not entirely unknown in Greek coinage, the best known comparison being the archaic eye on the fifth-century BCE coinage of Skione. This parallel is purely formal, however: the Skione type belongs to an entirely different cultural, artistic, and religious setting, and there is no comparable reason to interpret its eye as representing the divine. descripcion_anverso: ★ From the collection of Teddy Kollek (1911-2007), Mayor of Jerusalem, Leu 86, 5 May 2003, 469 ★ JUDAEA, Hellenistic Period (Yehud). Yeḥizqiyah (Hezekiah), circa 320-312 BCE (?). 1/4 Obol (Silver, 7 mm, 0.17 g, 4 h). [Youthful male head facing slightly to right on Macedonian shield].
descripcion_reverso: 𐤄𐤐𐤇𐤄 - 𐤉𐤇𐤆𐤒𐤉𐤄 ('Hezekiah, the governor' in Paleo-Hebrew) Owl standing right, head facing. Bromberg I 3. Hendin 10. Jeselsohn 105 ff. Meshorer, AJC, 10. Samel 2006. Shoshana I 20075. Sofaer 18-20. YC Type 24 (O12/R15). Attractive iridescent toning and with an exceptionally complete reverse. The obverse struck fully off center, otherwise, good very fine.From the collection of Teddy Kollek (1911-2007), Mayor of Jerusalem, Leu 86, 5 May 2003, 469 (with original ticket).Yeḥizqiyah is the most prominently attested named issuing authority in the late fourth-century coinage of Yehud. On the present specimen, both his name, YḤZQYH, and his title, HPḤH ('the governor'), are exceptionally clear, providing unusually direct evidence for his official authority. Gitler, Lorber, and Fontanille interpret the renewed appearance of name and title as indicating that Yeḥizqiyah had been formally confirmed, or reconfirmed, in office and that his authority was delegated by a higher political power. The male head set within a Macedonian shield (here off flan) gives the issue an explicitly military character, and the authors suggest that this coinage may have been struck to pay military or paramilitary units.Dated approximately to 320-312 BCE, the issue belongs to the turbulent age of the Diadochi, when Judaea lay at a strategic junction between Egypt and the territories contested first in the struggles involving Ptolemy and Perdikkas, and later between the Ptolemies and the Antigonids. Numismatic evidence suggests that Yeḥizqiyah’s career extended across the transition from Achaemenid to Macedonian rule, making him a rare example of a local official who may have retained authority through successive imperial regimes.The authors regard his identification with the elderly high priest Hezekiah mentioned by Pseudo-Hecataeus and Josephus (Pseudo-Hecataeus, apud Josephus, Contra Apionem 1.184–189) as plausible and highly attractive, though the discrepancy between the titles 'governor' and 'high priest' remains unresolved. They therefore allow either that the literary tradition misrepresented a secular governor as a high priest, or that Yeḥizqiyah may eventually have combined the highest civil and priestly offices. On their reconstruction, he left Judaea in late 312 or early 311 BCE, probably as a deportee under Ptolemy I, after which the coinage appears to reflect a period of administrative instability. descripcion_anverso: ★ An extremely rare Mnaieion from Ioppe, plate coin in CPE ★ PTOLEMAIC KINGS OF EGYPT. Arsinoe II, wife of Ptolemy II, died 270 BC. Mnaieion or Oktadrachm (Gold, 27 mm, 27.81 g, 12 h), Ioppe, struck under Ptolemy II, RY 33 = 253/2. Veiled head of Arsinoe II to right, wearing diademed stephane and ram's horn and with a lotus-tipped scepter over her left shoulder.
descripcion_reverso: ΑΡΣΙΝΟΗΣ ΦΙΛΑΔΕΛΦΟΥ Double cornucopiae bound with fillet and containing pyramidal cakes, pomegranate, and other fruits, and with two grape bunches hanging at sides; across lower field, ΛΓ (date) and monogram of IOΠ. CPE 667 ( this coin cited and illustrated on pl. 51 ). SNG Copenhagen -. Svoronos -. Troxell, Arsinoe, Group 3, -. Extremely rare. A few faint marks and with minor die rust on the obverse, otherwise, good very fine.Ex UBS 78, 9 September 2008, 1065 (with original ticket).The royal Ptolemaic mint at Ioppe opened in 261/0 BCE. The regnal-year dates show that Ioppe struck tetradrachms annually, while extremely rare mnaieia were issued in the 25th and 33rd regnal years of Ptolemy II, that is, in 261/0 and, as in the case of our piece, 253/2 BCE. Lorber points out that the royal mints of Ake-Ptolemais, Ioppe, Gaza, Tyre, and Sidon sometimes employed the same control marks, suggesting a degree of coordination between the different mints. Indeed, the obverse die of our mnaieion was also used at Tyre; cf. Lorber, p. 117. Presumably, the very small size of these issues did not justify the cutting of separate dies, so that dies – and probably mint personnel as well – were sometimes transferred between mints. descripcion_reverso: [HPΩΔ]OY - TETPA[PXOY] Palm frond; L - ΛZ (date) across field. Bromberg I 33. Hendin 6243. Meshorer, AJC, 14. RPC I 4931. Samel 2117-2118. Shoshana I 20118. Sofaer 105-106. Repatinated, otherwise, very fine.From 'A very interesting collection of coins of the Jews and the Southwestern Levant', Numismatica Ars Classica 59, 4 April 2011, 1331 (with original ticket).According to the Gospel of Luke, Pontius Pilate sent Jesus to Herod Antipas because, as a Galilean, he fell under the tetrarch’s jurisdiction; Antipas was then in Jerusalem for Passover. Antipas questioned Jesus, subjected him to mockery, and returned him to Pilate without passing sentence (Luke 23:6–12). Since this episode is recorded only by Luke, modern scholarship remains cautious about its precise historical basis: such an encounter is possible, but cannot be independently confirmed. The legal authority and immediate responsibility for the crucifixion rested with the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, not with Antipas. Dated to 33/4 CE, this coin was struck in close chronological proximity to the later of the two principal dates proposed for the crucifixion, 33 CE, the other being 30 CE (see lot 192 above). descripcion_reverso: [ΗΡ]ΩΔΗϹ [ΤΕΤΡΑΡΧΗϹ] Palm tree; ETO/C - MΓ (date) across field. Bromberg I 34. Hendin 6246. Meshorer, AJC, 17. RPC I 4934. Samel 2119. Shoshana I 20119. Sofaer 110. Rare. Areas of weakness and somewhat rough, otherwise, about very fine.Ex Leu 86, 5 May 2003, 491 (with original ticket).This coin, dated to regnal year 43 (39/40 CE), is the largest denomination in Antipas’ final issue and bears a dedication to Gaius Caesar Germanicus, the Roman emperor better known as Caligula (37–41 CE). During this same regnal year, Antipas and his wife Herodias approached Caligula at Baiae to seek the royal title, but her brother Agrippa I countered by accusing the tetrarch of conspiring against Rome and maintaining a vast stockpile of arms. Gaius consequently stripped Antipas of his tetrarchy and property, transferred them to Agrippa, and condemned him to perpetual exile (Josephus, Ant. 18.240–255; B.J. 2.181–183). He was exiled to the western provinces, probably to Lugdunum Convenarum in southwestern Gaul, although Josephus’ accounts are contradictory. The emperor honoured on this coin was thus also the ruler who, shortly afterwards, brought Antipas’ long reign to an abrupt end. descripcion_anverso: ★ An unusually attractive rendering of the Augusteum of Panias ★ JUDAEA, Herodians. Herod IV Philip, with Augustus, 4 BCE-34 CE. AE (Bronze, 21 mm, 9.74 g, 11 h), Caesarea Panias (Caesarea Philippi), RY 12 = 8/9 CE. ΚΑΙϹΑΡΙ ϹЄΒΑϹΤΩ Laureate head of Augustus to right.
descripcion_reverso: ΦΙΛΙΠΠΟΥ ΤΕΤΡΑΡΧΟΥ The Augusteum of Panias: Tetrastyle temple with stairs leading to it and pellet in pediment (clupeus virtutis?); L-I-B (date) between columns. Bromberg I 35. Hendin 6252. Meshorer, AJC, 3. RPC I 4940. Samel 2122. Shoshana I 20124. Sofaer 118. Well centered and with an unusually attractive rendering of the Augusteum of Panias. The obverse somewhat smoothed, otherwise, very fine.From 'A very interesting collection of coins of the Jews and the Southwestern Levant', Numismatica Ars Classica 59, 4 April 2011, 1336 (with original ticket).The tetrastyle temple on the reverse is generally identified as the Augusteum of Panias, the sanctuary of Augustus erected by Herod the Great near the sources of the Jordan and later incorporated into Philip’s capital, Caesarea Philippi. Philip’s coinage marked a decisive break with Hasmonean and earlier Herodian practice: he was the first Jewish ruler to place portraits of both the Roman emperor and himself on his coins, in striking contrast to the aniconic conventions commonly associated with the biblical prohibition of graven images.On the present issue, struck in regnal year 12 (8/9 CE), the portrait and name of Augustus dominate the obverse, while the reverse depicts the imperial cult temple but identifies the issuer as ΦΙΛΙΠΠΟΥ ΤΕΤΡΑΡΧΟΥ and dates the coin according to Philip’s own reign. The design thus acknowledges Roman supremacy and the cultic honours paid to the emperor while simultaneously asserting Philip’s local authority as tetrarch. Few coins of the Herodian dynasty express the political logic of Roman client rule more clearly. descripcion_anverso: ★ The first portrait of a Jewish ruler ever to appear on a coin ★ JUDAEA, Herodians. Herod IV Philip, 4 BCE-34 CE. AE (Bronze, 12 mm, 1.84 g, 11 h), Caesarea Panias (Caesarea Philippi), RY 34 = 30/1 CE. ΦΙΛΙΠΠΟΥ Bare-headed and draped bust of Herod IV Philip to right.
descripcion_reverso: L ΛΔ within wreath. Bromberg I 38. Hendin 6263. Meshorer AJC, 12. RPC I 4950. Samel -. Shoshana -. Sofaer 143. Very rare and among the finest known examples of this highly important issue, bearing the first portrait of a Jewish ruler ever to appear on a coin. Good very fine.Privately acquired from UBS, and previously privately acquired from Steve Rubinger (Antiqua, with original ticket).Although the Second Commandment’s prohibition of graven images did not constitute an absolute ban on all figural art, it fostered a strong aniconic tradition in Jewish coinage, and both the Hasmoneans and the earlier Herodian rulers had refrained from placing human portraits on their coins. Herod IV Philip broke decisively with this convention by introducing portraits of Augustus, Tiberius and Livia, thereby expressing Roman supremacy and his own subordinate position as a client ruler with unprecedented clarity. More remarkable still, he also placed his own likeness on his coinage, creating the earliest known numismatic portrait of a Jewish ruler.On the present issue, dated to regnal year 34 (30/1 CE), Philip reserved his own portrait for the smallest denomination. Whereas the larger denominations depict members of the imperial household and refer directly to Roman authority, this diminutive coin bears only Philip’s portrait and name, with his regnal date enclosed within a wreath on the reverse. Its modest size therefore belies its exceptional historical importance: by presenting Philip himself in the Greco-Roman tradition of ruler portraiture, it marks an even more radical break with Jewish numismatic convention than his adoption of portraits of the Roman imperial family.The coin thus represents not merely an abandonment of earlier aniconic restraint, but a striking assertion of Philip’s individual identity through the visual language of the wider Greco-Roman world. Struck in 30/31 CE, it also belongs to the period traditionally associated with Jesus’ public ministry and may have been issued in the same year as the earlier of the two principal dates proposed for the crucifixion, although this association remains secondary to the coin’s fundamental numismatic significance. Repatinated, otherwise, nearly very fine.Ex Sternberg XXXIV, 22-23 October 1998, 565 (with original auction flip).This issue bears no regnal date, but it was probably the large denomination accompanying the coins of Tiberius (Hendin 6259; RPC I 4948) and Livia (Hendin 6262; RPC I 4949), both dated to regnal year 34 of Herod IV, and should therefore likewise be dated to 30/1 CE. This is of particular interest because the two principal dates proposed for the crucifixion of Jesus are 30 and 33 CE (see lots 192-193 above). The coin may thus have been struck contemporary to the earlier of these two proposed dates.
